headline: Canada and U.S. Resume Talks Over Trump Tariffs as a New Deadline Looms
article_summary: While President Trump has declared that the two countries effectively have a deal, they remain apart on several key issues.
article_body: Canadian officials headed back to Washington on Thursday morning for another round of talks, in an effort to avert damaging new tariffs set to take effect Saturday morning and preserve Canada’s biggest trade relationship. Dominic LeBlanc, the Canadian minister in charge of U.S. trade, and Janice Charette, the chief trade negotiator, met with Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, shortly after noon in Mr. Greer’s offices, Mr. LeBlanc’s office said. Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada and his officials must now decide whether to accept a proposed American trade deal that falls well short of what they are seeking, or risk the United States imposing 50 percent tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in Canadian exports. On Tuesday night, President Trump suspended the sweeping new tariffs and announced that the two countries had reached a deal requiring only that some details and paperwork be worked out. But if Canada does not finalize the pact by early Saturday morning, new tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian exports will take effect. People in the United States and Canada who are familiar with the negotiations said talks are still very much underway and go well beyond tying off loose ends. The sticking points center on the three key Canadian industries that Mr. Trump hit with tariffs of up to 50 percent last year: steel, aluminum and lumber. In the talks, the U.S. has discussed reducing tariffs on some Canadian steel and aluminum exports to 25 percent from 50 percent, two people familiar with the plans said. That would still be about twice the rate Canada is seeking. Canadian steel exports would also face a quota under which only a certain volume would qualify for the proposed lower tariff, another person familiar with the negotiations said. Domestically, the Trump administration is facing a backlash to the proposal from U.S. steel mills, which have argued that the change would undercut their production. For the auto sector, a tariff that Mr. Trump imposed last year could be lowered to 15 percent from 25 percent, with a discount for the value of American parts, three other industry executives said. One person briefed on the talks said that Canada is pushing back against the proposal on autos. He said it appeared that the United States picked 15 percent to match the tariff Mr. Trump imposed on Japanese and Korean autos. Because the U.S. side has been unyielding on the rate, the person said that Canada is proposing to effectively lower the tariff by giving credit for Canadian parts as well as American ones. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Mr. Trump’s current auto tariffs have shattered free trade in the sector, which dates to 1965 and has made the industry highly integrated across the border. Mr. Trump has repeatedly described Canadian-built autos as products that the United States should not import. Negotiators have also been discussing important rules governing the North American auto industry under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement. The Trump administration has proposed raising the requirement for how much of a car’s content must come from North America to 82 percent from the current 75 percent, as well as requiring 50 percent of a car’s materials to come from the United States. Canada and Mexico have both opposed the idea of a U.S.-specific content requirement. Industry executives say they view the U.S. proposal as an opening position that will likely be negotiated down. Still, the U.S. effort to reorder the rules of the North American auto industry could be harmful to Canadian interests. Several people in the auto industry, as well as experts, say that a 15 percent tariff on autos will gradually doom the industry in Canada. Historically, the auto trade between the two countries has had a slight surplus for the United States. Over the last decade or so, exports to Canada from the three Detroit-based automakers have declined considerably, leaving Toyota and Honda as by far the largest producers in the country. Since Mr. Trump returned to office, Stellantis has moved production of a new Jeep from Ontario to Illinois, leaving a Canadian factory empty. General Motors closed an electric van factory and reduced its pickup truck assembly line in Ontario to one shift. Honda canceled plans for a major expansion in Canada to produce electric vehicles and batteries but recently announced plans to build a new factory in the United States. Flavio Volpe, the president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association of Canada, said that after accounting for American parts, a 15 percent tariff effectively becomes a 7.5 percent tariff. But the profit margin on most autos is about 6 percent, he said. He added that the U.S. content discount would likely force companies to source more American parts, to the detriment of the Canadian industry. Greig Mordue, a former executive at Toyota’s Canadian manufacturing operations, said that a 10 percent tariff might make Canadian factories marginally profitable but would not halt their gradual disappearance, despite the difficulty and expense of moving production. “It becomes a long-term bleed, “ he said, adding that with any auto tariffs, the “trajectory is not positive at any level.” The outcome of talks between the United States and Canada has important implications for Mexico, which is negotiating separately with the Trump administration on the future of the U.S.M.C.A. Marcelo Ebrard, the Mexican economy secretary, returned to the U.S. trade representative’s office Wednesday for more discussions, following meetings the evening before. Those talks centered on the sectoral tariffs that the Trump administration has levied on cars and car parts, as well as how the U.S.M.C.A. rules governing auto trade could change, a person familiar with the meetings said. Canada does appear to have agreed to one U.S. demand: an end to the boycott of American wine and spirits by government-owned liquor systems in eight of 10 Canadian provinces. In a virtual meeting with Canada’s premiers on Wednesday, Mr. Carney asked those who have banned the sale of U.S. liquor to restore it, according to Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia.
image_caption: Dominic LeBlanc, the Canadian minister in charge of U.S. trade, arriving to meet with Jamieson Greer, the U.S. trade representative, on Thursday in Washington. The ArcelorMittal Dofasco steel plant in Hamilton, Ontario. Cars parked outside the GM Assembly plant in Oshawa, Ontario.

headline: Where A.I. Is Creating Jobs for Humans — For a While
article_summary: In the fast-growing field of data annotation, workers in a small city in south India train A.I. to improve how it performs tasks traditionally done by people.
article_body: Evidence of the artificial intelligence boom often looks like the squat, windowless data centers that house acre after acre of hardware. But near the southern tip of India, the city of Karur is teeming with signs of A.I.’s ascendancy in human form. Hundreds of tech lab workers clog the streets on coffee breaks late on any given weekday afternoon — men and women in their 20s, corporate ID cards dangling from lanyards around their necks. Others work a few hours a weekend from home, supplementing their income by strapping iPhones to their heads and pressing record while they chop vegetables or make the bed. They work in a fast-growing field of A.I. called data annotation, which — for the moment, at least — requires a human touch. As the sentient backstop for artificial intelligence, data annotators help fix bugs and find blind spots in A.I. models, improving and refining the programs that steer your car, automate an assembly line and track inventory in retail stores. The work can be rote and less complex than what engineers train for in college, requiring hours in front of a screen to examine video frame by frame. But as A.I. capabilities change how companies design and produce products — making jobs like coding disappear for college graduates — data annotation is showing how countries like India, with entry-level job shortages and large youth populations, are adapting.
image_caption: In India, some people are strapping cameras to their bodies to collect data on how humans move and train A.I. A contractor wearing a smartphone attached to a harness to record her daily activities at her home in Karur. Humans help train artificial intelligence to better perform tasks like chopping vegetables.

headline: Trump’s Order to Cut Military Exercises With South Korea Carries Risks, Experts Say
article_summary: President Trump’s decision to curtail the military exercises came as allies question the U.S. commitment to longstanding alliances.
article_body: For years, the U.S. and South Korea militaries have participated in one of the largest military exercises in the world, with thousands of troops from both countries preparing for possible North Korea aggression. On President Trump’s orders, the Pentagon curtailed this year’s exercises and scaled back some live-fire components of the drill, which were already underway. Current and former military officials say the move is likely to undercut U.S. military readiness in the region at a time when allies are questioning the Trump administration’s commitment to longstanding partnerships and countering China. The president’s decision is also unlikely to affect the person he hoped to sway: North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jong-un. The exercises, called Ulchi Freedom Shield, usually run for 11 days and have sometimes included 17,000 or more U.S. troops and 50,000 South Korean troops. In past years, the sessions have featured some computer simulations carried out in a large bunker south of the capital, Seoul, intended to check the allies’ readiness to repel a North Korean attack. This year, some 18,000 South Korean troops were to take part in Ulchi Freedom Shield. The Pentagon has not said how many American troops had been expected to participate. While both countries have insisted that the exercises were defensive in nature, Mr. Kim has long called them provocative. North Korea’s Foreign Ministry has condemned the drills as “a rehearsal for an aggressive war.” The country conducted two ballistic missile tests off its east coast this month, vowing to “respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent.” Mr. Trump seemed to agree with North Korea, saying in a post on Sunday that the country under Mr. Kim had been “unthreatening and respectful” while he has been president. American troops have been through this before. Mr. Trump abruptly canceled the exercise in 2018 during his first administration, without notifying Defense Secretary Jim Mattis. At the time, Trump administration officials said they wanted to give negotiations meant to rein in North Korea’s nuclear ambitions an opportunity to succeed. Mr. Trump met with Mr. Kim three times but ultimately failed in that goal. Back then, officials said the military could weather one big interruption in the exercise schedule but that readiness would suffer if the drills lapsed for several years. After Mr. Trump’s announcement on Sunday, the Pentagon declined to say which specific training events would be canceled, modified or conducted through computer simulation. But former commanders said two main components would be affected: the testing of high-level command problems and other issues, and training for large scale, on-the-ground live fire and troop maneuvering. Both are valuable from a military readiness perspective, commanders said. A Pentagon official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss operational matters, said the American and South Korean militaries would continue training on their own before the exercise ends on Aug. 21, but that they would not train together as had been previously scheduled. “Of course it hurts readiness,” said Victor Cha, the Korea chair at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “And readiness relates to deterrence. If the Chinese or North Koreans feel that U.S. deterrence is not as strong, they might think there are opportunities there.” Mr. Cha also disputed the notion that canceling the exercises would help Mr. Trump to get a nuclear deal with North Korea, pointing to the 2018 talks that ultimately collapsed in Hanoi in 2019 over disagreement about relief from U.S. economic sanctions and the scope of North Korea’s nuclear disarmament. Gen. Curtis M. Scaparrotti, a retired top commander of U.S. forces in South Korea, said that scaling back live-fire training hurts troops’ ability to hone their combat skills. “It develops competence and confidence by training just as you would fight an adversary as a team,” General Scaparrotti said in an email. “The use of live rounds and rigorous training standards in training is the most realistic test of unit readiness.” In a rambling social media post on Sunday, Mr. Trump complained that South Korea had not supported the Trump administration in its war against Iran. He also said the military exercises were expensive, “with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!).” The estimated cost of this year’s exercise was $6.9 million, the Pentagon official said, adding that any savings resulting from the changes have not yet been determined. But former commanders said the vast majority of those costs had already been paid, for expenses like U.S. troop movements in and out of South Korea. South Korea’s Foreign Ministry appeared to be caught off guard by Mr. Trump’s announcement but pledged to continue coordinating with the United States on the military exercises. As the war with Iran sinks into a quagmire, Mr. Trump is increasingly refocusing on North Korea, which is now a de facto nuclear power. Mr. Trump posted a picture of himself with the North Korean leader on social media at least twice in recent months. “Kim Jong Un and I get along GREAT!” Mr. Trump wrote alongside a photograph he posted on Saturday of their meeting at the border between North and South Korea in 2019. Mr. Trump said on Wednesday that he planned to meet with Mr. Kim sometime later this year, but he did not offer details. “I get along with Kim Jong Un very well,” Mr. Trump said. “He’s going to be fine. As long as we have a smart president, he’s going to be fine.” Kim Yo Jong, the North Korean leader’s younger sister and close adviser, told state media on Wednesday that the country’s position toward the United States had not changed despite Mr. Trump’s decision to cut short the military exercises.
image_caption: American and South Korean troops participating in the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises last year. President Trump meeting with the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un in 2019.

headline: 36 Hours in the Cotswolds
Missile Barrage Shows Russia’s Doubt That Ukraine Can Defend Itself
article_summary: Moscow is taking advantage of Ukraine’s depleted stock of interceptors and is intensifying attacks, worsening the civilian death toll.
article_body: For much of the war, Russia’s air assaults followed a battle-tested formula : first, waves of drones to saturate and tie up air defenses; then, once a path was cleared, a salvo of highly destructive missiles. But as Ukraine now struggles with severe air defense shortages , Russia is going straight for the missiles. Overnight on Thursday, it opened a deadly air assault with a volley of ballistic missiles that resulted in several explosions across Kyiv, the capital, suggesting that some had hit their targets. The change in tactics is a sign that the Russian military is growing more confident of penetrating Ukrainian defenses, after weeks of attacks that have depleted Ukraine’s stocks of interceptors . In some of Russia’s overnight barrages, the Ukrainian military has been unable to shoot down a single ballistic missile. The Ukrainian authorities recently stopped releasing data on interception rates of these missiles, concerned about the alarming headlines it was generating. But the impact of Thursday’s attack was evident in the death toll and physical damage. At least 15 people were killed and about 40 injured in strikes that also damaged 30 residential buildings, a school and a children’s hospital, according to Ukrainian officials. Explosions erupted across the Ukrainian capital shortly before midnight as the bombardment rained down. The thundering reverberated down to a subway station where some of the city’s three million residents had taken shelter, pitching tents and laying mats on the granite platform. Worried that the gaps in aerial defenses have left them increasingly exposed, many Kyiv residents now spend several nights a week sheltering underground in subway stations and parking lots. Nearly 40,000 residents stayed in the capital’s subway stations overnight, according to the local authorities on Thursday.
image_caption: More than a dozen people were killed in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, in an overnight Russian missile barrage, Ukrainian officials said on Thursday.

headline: State Dept. Declares U.S. Citizen in China Wrongfully Detained
article_summary: U Min Zin, a scholar who studied Myanmar, is one of two U.S. citizens the department has designated as wrongfully detained in China.
article_body: The State Department on Thursday designated an American scholar arrested in China on spying charges in June as having been wrongfully detained. The detained U.S. citizen, U Min Zin, disappeared in China’s Yunnan province after traveling there to attend an academic conference at the invitation of the Chinese government, according to the State Department. “We call on Beijing to release all U.S. citizens arbitrarily detained or exit banned in China,” Dylan Johnson, the assistant secretary of state for global affairs, wrote on social media. “The safety and security of U.S. citizens is the State Department’s top priority.” The official designation comes about a month before President Trump is expected to host President Xi Jinping of China for an official visit, following Mr. Trump’s trip to Beijing this spring. It also comes as U.S. allies in the Asia-Pacific region have grown increasingly concerned about the United States’ willingness to help defend them against China and its partners, after Mr. Trump and the Pentagon recently scaled back major military exercises with South Korea. Mr. Min Zin is a political scientist and the executive director of a strategy and policy group founded in Myanmar, though it moved its headquarters after a 2021 military coup in that country, formerly known as Burma. The Chinese province where he was detained borders Myanmar. Mr. Min Zin, who was living in Thailand, has written on the politics of Myanmar for the opinion section of The New York Times, among other U.S. news organizations. His arrest took place less than two weeks before President Min Aung Hlaing of Myanmar made a five-day visit to China, and less than three weeks after Mr. Trump’s state visit to Beijing. Since returning to the Oval Office, Mr. Trump has adopted a warmer stance toward China, in pursuit of what both Trump and Xi administration officials have labeled “constructive strategic stability” between the two economic and military powerhouses. Mr. Min Zin’s arrest has complicated that trajectory. He is currently one of two U.S. citizens in China to have been officially declared by the State Department as wrongfully detained. The other, Youlin Chen, a seismologist, was detained at a Beijing airport in 2024 while trying to return to the United States. Under statute, the U.S. government is obligated to treat people it declares as wrongfully detained abroad as hostages of a foreign government and to work to secure their release. The cases are referred to the special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, and congressional committees are notified and periodically updated. Dr. Chen’s family said this year that Mr. Trump pressed his case with Mr. Xi when the two leaders met in Beijing. The group Mr. Min Zin led, the Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar, praised the State Department’s move and urged the Trump administration to make his detention “a top priority, particularly ahead of President Xi’s visit to meet with President Trump next month.” “This designation also reaffirms that independent, open-source researchers and academics should be able to conduct their work without fear of intimidation or arbitrary detention,” the group said in a statement.
image_caption: The detained U.S. citizen U Min Zin disappeared in China’s Yunnan province after traveling there to attend an academic conference at the invitation of the Chinese government, according to the State Department.

headline: First U.S. Deportees Arrive in Liberia, and Liberians Want Explanations
article_summary: Critics in the small West African nation say their government has not said why it agreed to one of the largest U.S. deportation deals, who the deportees are, or how they will be handled.
article_body: The first group of U.S. deportees arrived in Liberia on Thursday, amid a growing backlash there, with critics saying the Liberian government’s deal with the Trump administration to accept 1,200 deportees is too large and too opaque. The deal with Liberia, in West Africa, is one of the largest struck by the Trump administration for so-called third-country deportations, meaning that the deportees are not being sent to their home countries. The majority of the countries making such agreements have been in Africa, including Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ghana and South Sudan, among others. Twenty deportees arrived at Roberts International Airport on Thursday afternoon, in the Liberian capital, Monrovia, according to the Liberian government.It is unclear if any of them have criminal records in the United States. But the agreement has sparked questions among Liberians about a lack of transparency. “The issue of deportations is raising many concerns that can’t be left unanswered,” said Adama Dempster, a human rights lawyer and activist in Liberia. “What conditions will they be held in? And how does Liberia benefit?” he said. “Liberians, we are hospitable people, we love strangers. But the government should explain this.” The deportees will initially be held in a government facility and be allowed to seek asylum in Liberia or return to their home countries, said Jerolinmek Matthew Piah, Liberia’s information minister. “They are being received as guests,” he said in a statement. He highlighted Liberia’s history of welcoming refugees and migrants, often deported to countries where they have no ties, as an explanation for the deal. Liberia’s government has said it did not demand or receive any compensation as part of the deportation deal with the Trump administration. Mr. Dempster said this was hard to believe, considering the economic challenges in a country where more than half of the six million people live in poverty. “What is more concerning is that the U.S. is sending 1,200, a high number. Liberia has a struggling economy where unemployment is high, what conditions will be put in place to help?” Thirty countries have made third-country deportation deals with the Trump administration, according to Human Rights First, a nonprofit group that tracks deportations. For several months, the administration pushed to send to Liberia Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran immigrant whose deportation case has become a symbol of the president’s crackdown on illegal immigration. Mr. Abrego Garcia spent months in a notorious prison built for terrorists after being deported to El Salvador last year. He was later returned to the United States, then faced human smuggling charges that were later thrown out by a federal judge in Nashville as an abuse of prosecutorial powers. U.S. and Liberian officials have not said whether Mr. Abrego Garcia was among the deportees sent to Liberia on Thursday. No information about the deportees’ records has been made public, fueling anxiety in Liberia, where crime centered on the drug trade has exploded in recent years. A crackdown by law enforcement has seen hundreds of millions of dollars of cocaine seized by officials. “It’s risky for us,” said Yarssah Jallah, 35-year-old food vendor in Monrovia. “We already have the drug issue here. We don’t know who is who.” On Wednesday, a former vice president, Jewel Taylor, was charged with drug trafficking and money laundering. She is the ex-wife of Charles Taylor, a former Liberian president and convicted war criminal. Mr. Piah, the information minister, said the deportees were not “criminals” and “not being prosecuted in any manner under United States or Liberian law.” But his denials have been met with skepticism among rights groups that say his statement does not adequately address whether the deportees had criminal records or were awaiting trial. The deal with the Trump administration has also raised questions about whether diplomatic pressure was applied on Liberia, a country with deep ties to the United States. Liberian history is rooted in America’s “Back to Africa” movement and the American Colonization Society, a group formed in 1816 by philanthropists, abolitionists as well as some slave owners. The group helped resettle free Black Americans in what would become Liberia. At Liberia’s independence, its constitution and flag were modeled on those of the United States. English is the country’s official language. Last year, Joseph Boakai, Liberia’s president, was one of five African leaders to meet with President Trump at the White House. The meeting caused a stir when Mr. Trump complimented Mr. Boakai on his English, asking him “Where did you learn to speak so beautifully?” Liberia’s economy and health system have been hit hard by cuts to American foreign aid, damaging perceptions of the United States, and fueling suspicions that Liberia was forced to negotiate from a position of weakness. “As a sovereign country, was it possible for President Joseph Boakai to have refused President Donald Trump’s offer of accepting those individuals?” asked Clara Mallah, a program officer at the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia, a civil society group based in the capital. “Why can’t America keep them? Why Liberia?”
image_caption: Monrovia, the capital of Liberia. The U.S. deportation deal with Liberia is one of the largest so-called third-country deportation agreements struck by the Trump administration so far. An anti-government protest in Monrovia, last year. President Trump meeting African leaders, including President Joseph Boakai of Liberia, far right, at the White House last year.

headline: A Prince at 26: Once-Secret Son of Belgian Royal Gains Legal Recognition
article_summary: Clément Vandenkerckhove was born to Belgium’s Prince Laurent before his marriage. He is now a prince himself, though he is not expected to have royal duties.
article_body: Prince Laurent of Belgium has formally recognized an adult son who was born before he was married and whom he had not acknowledged publicly until last year. The prince established legal ties to his son, Clément Vandenkerckhove, 26, before a civil registrar in February, Soir Mag, a weekly magazine in Belgium, reported on Wednesday . Mr. Vandenkerckhove was also present and signed the documents, the magazine reported. The move made Mr. Vandenkerckhove a prince, though he is not expected to have any royal duties. Belgium’s Royal Palace confirmed to The New York Times that Prince Laurent had legally acknowledged his paternity of Mr. Vandenkerckhove but did not comment further, saying it was a private matter. Mr. Vandenkerckhove is the child of Prince Laurent and Iris Vandenkerckhove, better known as Wendy Van Wanten, a Belgian model, singer and actress. Prince Laurent, the younger brother of Belgium’s monarch, King Philippe, has three other children with his wife, Princess Claire of Belgium, whom he married in 2003. Under the terms of a 2015 royal decree, Mr. Vandenkerckhove is granted the title of prince but he will not be in line for the throne or have royal duties, according to Christian Behrendt, a professor of constitutional law at University of Liège in Belgium. People can enter the line of succession only if they are born in a marriage that is approved by a government decree, Professor Behrendt said. Prince Laurent said in a statement last September that Mr. Vandenkerckhove was his biological son. The announcement was “based on a sense of understanding and respect for those involved,” he said at the time .

headline: The Parents Are MAGA. The Kids Are Liberal. Can YouTube Help?
article_summary: “The Necessary Conversation,” a podcast and YouTube show, is a very public example of the political disputes families are having all across the country.
article_body: Every Sunday, the Kultgen-Popp family gathers on Zoom and yells at one another. From California and Texas, the adult siblings Chad Kultgen and Haley Popp try to convince their parents, Mary Lou and Bob Kultgen, that President Trump is evil. And from their living room in Oklahoma, their parents reject every argument. The family members lob contradictory headlines at one another, trading irreconcilable claims about the war in Iran, the Epstein files and other breaking news stories. These arguments always end with each exhausted family member saying, “I love you.” Then Chad, 50, who generally leads these debates, shares the video on YouTube in the form of a podcast called “ The Necessary Conversation ,” typically drawing more than 100,000 viewers an episode . For years, politics has been straining, and breaking, relationships. More than a third of Americans say political differences have led to breakups with family members, romantic partners, friends and co-workers, according to a 2026 study by psychologists at the University of California, Irvine. In December 2025, 56 percent of Americans surveyed by the Pew Research Center said they’d stopped talking to someone about political or election news because of something they said — up from 45 percent in 2024. The internet is awash in steel-cage-match-style debates such as Jubilee shows or “ Change My Mind ,” where strangers try to roast each other for the audience’s entertainment. But “The Necessary Conversation” stands out as a public manifestation of something families have been doing in private all over the country. And family fights can cut more deeply than a sparring match with a stranger. For the Kultgen-Popp family, at least, fighting feels like progress. In Trump’s first term, after Chad posted anti-Trump memes on Facebook, his mother blew up at him and the family went no-contact for something approaching a year. They were too angry to talk politics — but too partisan to avoid the subject altogether.
image_caption: For Chad Kultgen and his family, fighting feels like progress. Chad Kultgen, with the microphone, generally leads the podcast debates. His parents, Bob and Mary Lou Kultgen. Chad’s sister, Haley Popp, at her bakery kitchen.

headline: Trump Threat Puts Focus on Iran’s Trading Partners
article_summary: President Trump appeared to suggest that the United States would impose economic penalties on countries that do business with Iran, though he did not specify what actions he would take.
article_body: President Trump has threatened “tremendous economic consequences” on any nation that does business with Iran, without offering details. The threat appeared to be his latest effort to isolate the country from the global economy and pressure its leadership into negotiating an end to the war. The United States has already imposed debilitating sanctions on Iran’s economy and its leadership, and the Trump administration has previously sanctioned certain foreign businesses and organizations that trade with Tehran. Mr. Trump’s vaguely worded social media post on Wednesday seemed to suggest that he could target nations that buy Iranian oil, without naming any. The president has, on occasion, backed down from such threats. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi of Iran dismissed his latest warning, calling it “a diversion” from America’s own crises. If Mr. Trump follows through, these are some of the countries that could be most affected: China is Iran’s largest trading partner and the primary consumer of its oil, according to recent analysis by the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a group founded by Congress to examine America’s bilateral ties to China. For years, China has been practically alone in its willingness to defy Western sanctions on Iranian oil, buying up to as much as 90 percent of Tehran’s oil exports. In recent months, however, Iran’s ability to ship oil by sea has been all but cut off by a U.S. naval blockade. Last year, China estimated its bilateral trade with Iran to be worth nearly $10 billion, a figure that doesn’t include oil.
