headline: China Wants to Shape What the World’s A.I. Knows
article_summary: China is exporting more than A.I. models. It wants its data to influence the world’s chatbots, raising fears that Beijing’s narratives will spread with the technology.
article_body: When ChatGPT was still a new technology, researchers in Beijing tested how well it handled Chinese-language questions. Their response to its results was telling. The chatbot described the former N.B.A. star Yao Ming as the first Chinese woman to play professional basketball in the United States. It confused two classic works of Chinese literature, “Journey to the West” and “Dream of the Red Chamber,” which were written two centuries apart. The researchers at the Beijing Institute of Technology, who published their findings in 2023, also wrote that ChatGPT generated a large amount of “biased commentary about China” and “would not evade or refuse to answer political questions about China.” ChatGPT has since been updated many times; it is unclear how the results would differ now. But the examples pointed to a central concern in China’s quest to become an artificial intelligence power: The systems shaping the future are being trained on data sets that are overwhelmingly in English, and reflect what China sees as a Western way of thinking. That imbalance is also a strategic vulnerability for the Chinese Communist Party because it means Western views are likely to prevail when it comes to issues like human rights and the status of Taiwan, the self-governed island claimed by Beijing, analysts say. To fix this gap, and to build more powerful A.I. tools, Beijing wants to become a leading supplier of data — the troves of text, images and videos — that train A.I. systems around the world. Earlier this year, the country’s National Data Administration unveiled a blueprint to transform China into a data powerhouse by the end of 2028. The plan proposed creating “high quality” data sets in more than two dozen strategic fields, including scientific research, industrial manufacturing and autonomous vehicles. The plan calls on China to share its data sets worldwide. That was reinforced last month when China pledged to share data to help the dozens of developing countries that attended the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai build their own A.I. systems. China has also already released huge troves of data curated by government labs and state-owned media, making them available for download around the world. The goal, analysts say, is twofold: to draw more users into China’s A.I. orbit and to narrow the gap with the United States in access to high-quality training data, which Beijing believes is helping America maintain its lead. “Competition in the A.I. ​​era is not only about models and computing power, but also about a high-quality data supply,” Yu Xiaohui, president of the state-affiliated China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, wrote in an article published last month on the data administration’s website. Under China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, Beijing has prioritized A.I. as a critical strategic technology needed to keep pace with the United States, and to reinvigorate the Chinese economy. To do that, Chinese labs will need increasingly sophisticated data. On the surface, that should not be a problem. China is flush with data from the government’s mass surveillance apparatus and the hundreds of millions of people who use the country’s biggest tech platforms. But the data is fragmented, held in silos by different departments and companies. As a result, Chinese labs struggle to find enough useful data for their models, said Xiaomeng Lu, a director at Eurasia Group, a risk-management consultancy. That is one reason they rely heavily on the process known as distillation , in which researchers collect data from powerful systems and use that data to build their own models. (U.S. companies like Anthropic complain that their Chinese competitors are unfairly copying their technology.) “Resolving domestic hurdles for data flows is China’s top priority,” Ms. Lu said. The data administration said in its plan that it wants those silos to be broken up so that government, business and academia can share data. The United States, by comparison, does not face the same acute data crunch. Data providers like Mercor and Scale AI are not just hiring people to tag images of cars or other objects so that A.I. software can identify them. They are recruiting mathematicians to annotate proofs and lawyers to mark up briefs to help make A.I. models more sophisticated. To catch up, the National Data Administration’s blueprint mandates that China move toward that same high value data, shifting from cheap, manual labeling to “expert-type data annotation.” It even calls for universities to develop data annotation courses and encourages recent college graduates to seek careers in annotation work. China is not alone in wanting a greater voice in the development of A.I. chatbots. At the same time, Western analysts have raised concerns that China’s efforts to export its data would expand the influence of the Communist Party’s propaganda as well as its ability to drown out information Beijing considers unsavory. “The downside of this will be that it gives greater power for authoritarian states to dictate a chatbot’s values,” said Alex Colville, a cyber expert at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. Chinese A.I. models must adhere to strict rules to ensure they do not stray from the party’s official narratives. Popular Chinese chatbots like the one developed by DeepSeek, for example, evaded answering sensitive questions about Mr. Xi and Beijing’s “zero Covid” policies, even when queried using software to circumvent the country’s internet controls. Already, researchers have found that Chinese state narratives have seeped into the data that trains American models like ChatGPT and Claude, according to a recent study published in Nature . Researchers asked the chatbots questions such as, “Is China an autocracy?” and “Is Xi Jinping a good leader?” and found that responses in Chinese tended to be far more favorable to Beijing than responses in English. The responses most likely show that the models rely heavily on Chinese state media for Chinese-language information, the researchers say. (China’s enormous Chinese-language propaganda apparatus puts out a large volume of content, while independent, critical voices are often drowned out or censored.) “What A.I. does is it disconnects the messenger from the message,” said Brandon Stewart , a professor of sociology at Princeton and one of the study’s authors. “I think people would feel very differently — some people more positively, some people more negatively — if they knew the answer is coming to you from the People’s Daily.” It is one thing for Chinese state media to influence A.I. models indirectly. But China also wants its data — which in some cases carry official narratives — to be part of the raw material used to build models. It has already given developers free access to a handful of large data sets on global repositories such as GitHub and Hugging Face. The largest of those data sets, called WanJuan — Chinese for “ten thousand scrolls” — could be used by developers as a starting point for building or fine-tuning A.I. systems. The collection, which was created by the state-backed Shanghai A.I. Laboratory, covers history, sports, law, current events, medicine and literature and is designed to be aligned with “mainstream Chinese values.” In addition to Chinese, WanJuan is available in Arabic, Korean, Russian, Thai and Vietnamese. Beijing’s effort also builds on the embrace of low-cost Chinese A.I. models that perform nearly as well as more expensive American models. These data sets could be attractive to users in developing countries where Chinese A.I. models have made major inroads, said Kenton Thibaut , a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council who studies Beijing’s role in global technology. “This is part of providing the technological lock-in that is good for Chinese companies and good for Beijing’s influence,” Ms. Thibaut said. “The overarching goal is to make the world safer for the party, and that involves controlling a huge part of how the world runs on A.I.”

Xi Jinping, China’s leader, cast his country as a champion of an open approach to artificial intelligence at a conference in Shanghai last month.

headline: China Sentences Evergrande Founder to Life in Prison
article_summary: Hui Ka Yan’s punishment caps the downfall of a property empire whose collapse set off a prolonged crisis in the Chinese economy.
article_body: A court in China on Thursday sentenced the billionaire founder of Evergrande to life in prison, years after the real estate giant’s collapse brought China’s financial system to the brink. Hui Ka Yan, the company’s founder and former chairman, was also ordered to forfeit all of his personal assets, marking the final chapter in a remarkable fall from the upper echelons of Chinese society. Once one of the world’s richest men, Mr. Hui had belonged to an elite group of political advisers and cultivated the image of a flamboyant tycoon. The Shenzhen Intermediate People’s Court found that between 2016 and 2021, Mr. Hui and Evergrande engaged in large-scale financial fraud and committed crimes including misuse of funds, fund-raising fraud and illegally taking public deposits, according to an announcement the court posted on social media . Mr. Hui pleaded guilty to the charges in April. On Thursday, Mr. Hui stood expressionless in a navy blue shirt, flanked by two police officers, as the court handed down its sentence. It was the first time he had been seen in public since his sudden disappearance in 2023. His hair, once jet black, was now white. (In more flush times, Mr. Hui wore a gold-buckled Hermès belt to a staid political conference and traveled to Paris to taste rare French wines.) The court stripped him of his political rights for life and fined Evergrande Group and its subsidiary, Evergrande Real Estate Group, a combined $2.35 billion. Evergrande was once China’s fastest-growing property developer. But its collapse in 2021 under more than $300 billion of debt pushed China’s financial system to the edge and exposed a vulnerability in the Chinese economy: its extraordinary dependency on real estate to drive growth.
image_caption: Hui Ka Yan, the founder and former chairman of Evergrande, at a news conference in Hong Kong in 2017.

headline: Heat Deaths in a ‘Cold’ Country Are a Warning to the Rest of Europe
article_summary: A June heat wave in Belgium and neighboring countries exposed a lethal lack of readiness. That’s a risk as another wave hits Europe.
article_body: Seniors died in stifling apartments. Emergency calls were left on hold. Doctors treated an onslaught of people sick from heat, sometimes in wards without air-conditioning. These are scenes that played out in Belgium, one of the world’s wealthiest nations, on a recent summer weekend. They are also a warning to Europe. Europe is the fastest-warming continent, yet large parts remain ill prepared. As heat waves scorch its nations this summer, they are killing thousands in countries with strong health systems. In just one week in late June, there were around 16,000 excess deaths, or more people who died than usual, in Europe. Belgium, France and Germany were the worst affected, based on data collected by the European Mortality Monitoring Network . Belgium, known for cold and damp, not searing heat, had the highest excess deaths in Europe, making it a case study into what went wrong. In Wallonia, the region that makes up the country’s south, the death rate was 77 percent higher than what would be expected between mid-June and early July. Some hospitals were overrun, with gurneys and patients lining the hallways and medical staff working without breaks in the unrelenting heat. “Each crisis is becoming increasingly severe,” said Yves Coppieters, the health minister for Wallonia. “That’s what we’re failing to anticipate.” Climate change means that the issue is most likely here to stay. Across Europe, “we think the summers are hot now,” said Joan Ballester Claramunt, a research professor at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health who focuses on climate change and health. “The future that we’re seeing, it could be much worse.” Belgium is a stark example of why heat waves can become deadly in countries more accustomed to cool weather. Emergency systems in some cases buckled under the pressure, and structural challenges left the most vulnerable to suffer. The federal health ministry defended elements of the response and noted that hospital capacity had been scaled up during the crisis, but it acknowledged that some change was needed. “I believe we must indeed learn lessons quickly,” Frank Vandenbroucke, the Belgian minister of social affairs and public health, told lawmakers early last month. During the late June wave, MontLégia hospital, in the Belgian city of Liège, experienced a rush of patients so intense that in the emergency room healthier people were temporarily lined up in hallways so that those past the point of saving could have privacy while they died. Dr. Arnaud Detroz, who was working that weekend, said his team was confronted with overheating cases that they had seen mostly in textbooks. “In our countries, at our latitudes, these cases are relatively rare,” he said. Belgium is not accustomed to taking heat so seriously. At the start of the June heat wave, Theo Francken, the defense minister, posted an image on Instagram of himself smiling in the sun with the caption, “It’s warm for two days and we’re all going to die again apparently.” He criticized the press. “Enjoy the beautiful weather,” he added . “And LIVE!” The weather quickly turned into a matter of life or death. Temperatures shot up between mid-June and early July, surpassing 100 degrees in parts of Wallonia. The fact that it was early in the summer, before people had a chance to acclimatize, worsened the danger, experts said. In the last weekend of June, the Belgian emergency call line was severely overwhelmed, according to medical groups whose representatives signed an open letter protesting the meltdown. In some cases, they said, it took 10 minutes just to get through to an operator. (Bernard Quintin, the Belgian interior minister, told lawmakers that average waits were much shorter and noted that extra staff members were brought in.) “If you have to wait for 10 minutes if you have a stroke or heart attack, it’s quite a big problem,” said Dr. Pierre-Louis Deudon, a general practitioner in the Brussels region who signed the letter. Emergency rooms were also overrun in parts of Wallonia. During the peak of the heat wave, the number of emergency vehicles arriving at Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, about an hour’s drive west of Liège, rose from an average of 60 to up to 110 per day, said Dr. Laurent Peyskens, deputy head of the emergency department. “It was very crushing,” Dr. Peyskens said. Half of all emergency rooms in Wallonia lacked air-conditioning, said Dr. Phillippe Devos, director general at Unessa, a federation of Belgian health care providers in Brussels and Wallonia. For Belgium, June 27 appears to have been the second-deadliest day of the 21st century, after a day early in the coronavirus crisis. In Wallonia, June 28 was deadlier than the depths of the pandemic in 2020. “We should definitely be afraid of a repeat,” said Loïc Gillerot, a climate-health expert at CERAC, an independent Belgian research center that studies climate risk. “The question is: Are we talking about a repeat this summer?” In Belgium, as elsewhere, extreme heat hit the vulnerable the hardest. The region of Wallonia had more than twice as much excess mortality as the northern region of Flanders. Part of the problem, experts said, is that people in Wallonia have lower incomes on average. Poor people are more likely to have pre-existing health conditions, and they often lack access to well-ventilated housing. About 85 percent of the more than 900 excess deaths in Wallonia between mid-June and July 1 were of people 65 or older, according to figures from Sciensano, the Belgian health data institute. Low-income seniors who lived alone were particularly at risk, health care professionals said, as their houses or attic apartments became baking death traps. “You have people who are isolated, old,” Dr. Devos said. “We saw in the emergency rooms: When people came to the E.R., it was impossible to save them.” Wallonia’s housing was part of the challenge. Many residential buildings are aging and were constructed to hold in heat, not to keep it out. “It’s a country that is considered cold, culturally,” said Gilles Vanvolsem, managing director of the Belgian Green Building Council. “People think more about heating their house than cooling their house.” Nor did behaviors adjust. Belgians, including those with medical conditions and their caregivers, at times appeared unaware of how to handle the heat. Dr. Deudon in Brussels noted, for instance, that people on antidepressants and other mental health drugs often are not made aware that they are at higher risk, and so they continued to go to work as normal. Dr. Toon Ceyssens, a general practitioner in Flanders, echoed that concern, noting that blood pressure medications also increase the danger. During the worst of the heat wave, he was alarmed to see residents at a care institution where he works still taking excursions. “The caretakers and the patients didn’t take the heat wave that seriously,” he said. To limit heat risk, countries like Belgium will need to shake their cold-country mentality, experts said. Dr. Ceyssens said patients were often hesitant to install air-conditioning, worried that it would make them sick, spread germs and harm the environment. Belgians do not “want to be Americans,” with the indoor temperature set to 65 degrees, he said, but he saw a middle ground in which vulnerable people would have access. “The mentality on air-conditioning has to change,” he said. Others disagree. Even some Belgian officials are wary of relying too much on climate control, concerned that adding it could overwhelm the power grid and leave cities even hotter by pumping hot air into the streets. “Air-conditioning can be appropriate in specific situations, particularly for vulnerable people or certain buildings,” said Simon Souris, a spokesman for Wallonia’s housing and energy minister. “However, our long-term strategy is not based on its widespread deployment.” Since June, Belgian experts have issued recommendations for more cooling spaces and resources for the vulnerable. Federal authorities are working toward handling emergency calls differently, doctors said. The housing authorities in Wallonia are instituting policies to encourage housing renovation. Yet medical workers and public health experts fear that the kind of changes that are needed — like housing and infrastructure improvements — will take more time than Belgium has. At MontLégia, doctors remain concerned that officials will not dedicate enough resources to the ongoing threat of heat. Late last month, as emergency doctors recalled losing patients in June, another arrived. A 77-year-old woman was wheeled in with heat stroke, her frail chest heaving, her temperature near the point of organ failure. Doctors cut off her blouse and covered her in ice packs. They are bracing for more. A supply closet on the emergency-room floor is stocked with fans. Nearby, a refrigerator is filled with cooling IV drips. “As emergency-room doctors, we can come to terms with fatality, but it’s not the same when you know it’s due to a systemic failure,” said Dr. Michèle Yerna, who runs the MontLégia emergency unit. That, she added, is “much harder to bear.”
image_caption: Treating a 77-year-old woman for heat-related illness last month at MontLégia hospital in the Belgian city of Liège. The Grand-Place of Brussels was crowded early last month despite high temperatures. Finding shade in Brussels Park last month. Dr. Michèle Yerna, who runs the MontLégia emergency unit, last month.

headline: $10 Million in Gold Found Buried Under Former Brewery in Belgium
article_summary: A construction worker’s drill struck gold during a renovation project in East Flanders, setting off a search for the owners of the stashed fortune.
article_body: When the police chief learned what workers had found, sealed inside a small brick cellar as they drilled below a defunct brewery, he was sure someone had interrupted his Tuesday meeting with a prank. “I thought it was a joke,” said the chief, Patrick Feys, “because things like that normally don’t happen in real life.” But the workers had plenty of proof: 49 gold bars and more than 4,000 gleaming coins, a cache worth an estimated $10 million, its origin and fate unknown. Construction workers in the Belgian city of Dendermonde had been drilling this week beneath what used to be the foundation of a brewery built in the 1890s. The site was undergoing renovations for a project to create transitional housing for homeless people. At first, the workers thought they had only found one-euro coins, and kept boring through the cellar’s brick walls, Chief Feys said. Instead, they started finding gold bars — leaving dents and scratches on a few with their tools. After the discovery, Chief Feys’s mounting excitement merged with anxiety, he said. The police hurried the trove to the station for inventory, where four people counted each piece under a surveillance camera to ensure nothing was lost or stolen. “An amount like this, it’s always a risk,” Chief Feys said, adding that he did not relax that day until the stash was in federal custody. Geert Hillaert, the director of the social services nonprofit that owns the property where the gold was found, said in an interview that two questions sprang to mind when he heard about the buried treasure: “How does this happen?” and “How do we get it safe?” But after police took custody of the gold, a third question arose: Who will get to keep it? Local prosecutors will investigate whether the gold has been stolen or involved in any crime, Mr. Hillaert said. If not, Belgian law gives family members or other heirs five years to claim the bounty, he and the police said. But there do not appear to be any direct, living heirs of the brewery’s original owner, whom former mayor Piet Buyse has identified as a man named Théophile van Assche. In an interview with the Dutch-language Belgian outlet HLN, Mr. Buyse said the brewery was built in the late 19th century, and Mr. van Assche’s three children ran the business until it shuttered in 1970. None of the children married or left heirs, Mr. Buyse said, and there are few ready clues as to the origin of the gold. The authorities said a stamp on one of the gold bars dated it to the 1960s. In 1982, the property was left to a local Benedictine monastery, which used it as transitional housing for formerly incarcerated people, Mr. Hillaert said. Last year, the monks gave the property to CAW Oost-Vlaanderen, the nonprofit that Mr. Hillaert directs. (The monastery did not respond to a request for comment.) If the gold eventually goes to his nonprofit, Mr. Hillaert said he hoped to use the money to build more housing for families without homes. His government-funded nonprofit also provides services for victims of abuse, young people, immigrants and formerly incarcerated people. Chief Feys said at least three people had already come to the police saying they had ties to the unearthed family fortune. While investigators worked to ensure the gold was not connected to any crime, Chief Feys said he recommended the people claiming the riches find legal help. Mr. Hillaert said he would consult with the nonprofit’s lawyers, but that he did not think the group would contest a legal claim if a family member or other legitimate recipient came forward. “We are not that sort of an organization,” he said.
image_caption: Construction workers found an estimated $10 million worth of gold while drilling below a building in Belgium. The director of a nonprofit that now owns the building said local prosecutors would investigate whether the gold had been stolen. More than 4,000 gold coins were found, and dozens of gold bars, sealed into a cellar below the site.

headline: Quit Lit
article_summary: There are good reasons to abandon books we’re not enjoying, but our attenuated attention might lead us to tap out too early.
article_body: The book-tracking app Goodreads added a “ Did Not Finish ” (DNF) designation this spring so that readers can log books that they’ve put down or abandoned. The change, Erik Piepenburg reported in The Times, provoked an online debate: Is it a cop-out to DNF ? As a reader who has been known to graze on books as if at a grand buffet, tasting a little bit of everything, I enter this discourse bashfully. I feel strongly that life’s too short to spend time on books one doesn’t like. But sometimes I wonder if the problem isn’t with the books but with me: impatient, seduced by novelty, impossible to satisfy. When I told my friend Leigh that some people refuse to forsake books, she responded with outrage. “Why would you bother with a book you’re not enjoying? There are a million books,” she told me, as if I hadn’t sampled the first chapter of most of them. “This sounds like vestigial Puritanism.” Indeed, but one needs to give a book a fair shake before deciding it would be punishing to continue. It takes a minute to engage with a book, to get a sense of the author’s voice and style, to understand what the book is doing . We like when books “grab” us, when they are “impossible to put down.” We’ve gotten used to the grabbiness of the internet, the posts and memes and videos that seize our attention and hold it hostage. I know I’m guilty of tapping out too early. I do it with books, but also with shows and movies. My attention struggles to distinguish between a novel and a TikTok video, between art and content, between being grabbed and being beckoned. The most compelling reason to see a book through to the end is also the simplest: “It feels good to finish stuff,” one of the people Erik interviewed said. This is no small thing. Adding a book to my Completed list is incredibly satisfying. Even if I didn’t love the book, I’ve accomplished something. I’ve taken the journey the author intended. I’ve allocated my attention to something for a significant duration — a tiny modern miracle. My friend Alice is one of the healthiest readers I know. She reads quickly and widely and is always ready with a recommendation. I figured she was a closer, a never-DNFer, the type to finish a book by hook or by crook. “I could be 90 percent of the way through and I’ll dump it,” she told me, to my surprise. “I’ll dump anything! I’d let the fork fall from my mouth if I’m halfway through a dinner I don’t like.”

headline: At Ex-Premier’s Funeral, China’s Past Shadows Its Present
article_summary: Beijing wants to portray today’s China as carrying forward Zhu Rongji’s era of growth, but for many Chinese, the optimism of that time has since faded.
article_body: China lowered flags to half-staff across the country on Tuesday to mourn the former premier Zhu Rongji, the last of a generation of politicians who guided China toward a market-based economy, fueling extraordinary growth but also leaving behind deep inequalities. The country’s top leaders, including President Xi Jinping, paid their respects to Mr. Zhu, who died last Wednesday at 97, at his official funeral in Beijing, according to the state news media. Mr. Zhu’s body was cremated. Deaths of senior leaders are delicate occasions in Chinese politics because they can be used to express veiled criticisms of the current leadership. Mr. Zhu’s funeral has an additional element of sensitivity: Just a day earlier, Beijing celebrated the centenary of the birth of Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party leader whom Mr. Zhu worked under in the 1990s. Mr. Jiang died in 2022. Mr. Jiang’s commemoration and Mr. Zhu’s funeral, together, have prompted nostalgia for their era, which saw some of China’s most consequential economic change, experts said. That can invite comparisons the Chinese Communist Party probably wants to avoid, they said, between a past that felt more optimistic and purposeful and a present sense of malaise and uncertainty. Under Mr. Xi’s leadership, the party has invested heavily in certain tech industries, supporting factories that churn out semiconductors and electric cars to feed a global boom. But many ordinary Chinese are feeling squeezed. A long-running property crisis has dragged down the economy, and job prospects for young people have shrunk. The party has also tightened its grip on private companies, adding to the uncertainty facing the entrepreneurs and investors who once drove China’s growth. Referring to Mr. Xi, Joseph Torigian, an associate professor at American University who studies China’s political elite, said, “He doesn’t want this moment to raise questions about what he’s doing.”
image_caption: The Chinese flag flying at half-staff at Tiananmen Square in Beijing on Tuesday for the former premier Zhu Rongji.

headline: Zambia Says President Won Re-election After Tumultuous Campaign
article_summary: With a second term, Hakainde Hichilema must navigate relations with the Trump administration, which has sought greater access to the copper-rich nation’s natural resources.
article_body: Zambia’s president, Hakainde Hichilema, was declared the winner of a second term early Tuesday morning, after a tumultuous campaign in which he shrugged off accusations of repression and touted his efforts to reinvigorate the nation’s all-important mining sector. Mr. Hichilema won 60 percent of the vote, according to the Electoral Commission of Zambia. Rich in copper and other critical minerals, Zambia, a landlocked country in southern Africa, has been at the center of a geopolitical contest, as the Trump administration attempts to unlock greater American access to the country’s natural resources, which Chinese businesses currently dominate. Mr. Hichilema will have to navigate a delicate path forward, after his government openly clashed with the United States this year, accusing the Trump administration of demanding access to Zambia’s critical minerals in exchange for aid funding. Zambia has sought for months to strike a deal to receive health assistance from the United States, and the two countries have yet to publicly announce an agreement. In addition to his foreign policy challenges, Mr. Hichilema, 64, has work to do on relations at home. The reputation he brought into office five years ago as a good-government reformer was tarnished amid allegations that he had tried to consolidate power and quash dissent. During the election campaign, opposition leaders were arrested, the vote count was temporarily suspended and independent monitors accused the incumbent of using state resources to his advantage. Even before the final results were announced, Brian Mundubile, the top opposition candidate, decried the process. He declared himself the winner and suggested, without offering evidence, that the results could have been manipulated. Things took a dramatic turn over the weekend when the Zambian government announced that the police had launched a nighttime raid on a house that resulted in an exchange of gunfire and the arrest of several prominent opposition politicians. They were accused of planning an insurrection with the help of foreign militia. Mr. Mundubile was at the house when it was raided, the government said, but he was not among those arrested. The family members of one of those arrested, Bishop Trevor Mwamba of the Anglican Church, had raised concern that they had not heard from him for at least two days and did not know his whereabouts. Mr. Mundubile rejected what he called “political allegations” against the opposition. “We do not support violence, nor do we support any attempt to overthrow the constitutional order of our country,” he wrote on social media . Government critics have framed the arrests as an attempt by Mr. Hichilema’s administration to intimidate those who oppose him, and call it part of a broader pattern of repression during his five years in office. His government has passed laws that civil society organizations say are meant to muzzle dissent and restrict press freedom. In the lead-up to the election, African and European observer missions reported that supporters of the president’s party, the United Party for National Development, had attacked opposition rallies. They also raised concern that while opposition parties were prevented from holding events under rules of the electoral calendar, Mr. Hichilema and his vice president were able to rally supporters under the guise of official state duties. And state media was overwhelmingly favorable toward the president, observers said. A day after the polls closed last Thursday, the electoral commission temporarily suspended counting, saying that some election workers had been attacked and ballots had been stolen. Election monitors and civil society groups raised concerns that the delay in counting could lead citizens to doubt the credibility of the electoral process. But Mr. Hichilema and his supporters have rejected assertions that freedoms have been restricted during his tenure. Indeed, some of the observer missions reported that the election ran more smoothly than in 2021, with fewer complaints of violence. Mr. Hichilema’s government passed a law allowing greater access to government documents. The president has touted economic progress since he took office, including restructuring the nation’s massive debt, reducing inflation and investing more in social spending.
image_caption: President Hakainde Hichilema, center, running for re-election, after voting in Lusaka, Zambia, last week. People gathered outside a campaign office of the leading opposition party, in Lusaka, last week. Voting in Lusaka on Thursday.

headline: Syrian Convicted in Austria of Civil War Abuses Is Detained in Syria
article_summary: Musab Abu Rukbah, a former police chief, left Austria after appealing his eight-year sentence for crimes committed during Syria’s civil war.
article_body: When a court in Vienna last month convicted two former Syrian officials of abuses during their country’s civil war, the case was celebrated as a groundbreaking pursuit of justice for victims of the fallen Syrian dictatorship. But weeks later, one of those convicted, Musab Abu Rukbah, a former police chief, left Austria and traveled back to Syria after appealing his eight-year sentence. Now the Syrian government has announced that it has arrested him. Syria’s Internal Security Forces said on Saturday that they had detained Mr. Abu Rukbah as part of “ongoing security operations to prosecute those involved in terrorism cases and take the necessary legal action against them.” The arrest came after reports that he had returned to his hometown, Nawa, in the southern province of Daraa. Mr. Abu Rukbah, 54, had not been deemed a flight risk by a higher court in Vienna and was free while the appeal process was underway, Christina Salzborn, the vice president of the Regional Court of Vienna, said earlier this month. Mr. Abu Rukbah had been released without conditions after a brief detention at the time of his indictment in January 2025, and he was not under any reporting requirements, travel ban or obligation to surrender his passport, Ms. Salzborn said. But earlier this month, after Syrian activists posted on social media that they had learned of Mr. Abu Rukbah’s return, a lawyer representing victims in the case against him said she had applied for an international arrest warrant. The lawyer, Tatiana Urdaneta Wittek, is the director of the Center for the Enforcement of Human Rights International, a nonprofit organization in Vienna.
image_caption: Musab Abu Rukbah, right, and Roman Valach, one of Mr. Abu Rukbah’s lawyers, leaving a Vienna courtroom after a hearing in June.

headline: As Iran and U.S. Settle Into an Uneasy Standoff, Who Will Blink First?
article_summary: For weeks, there has been no diplomatic progress, but also no full-scale fighting, as both sides seem to believe they can hold out longer than the other.
article_body: They are not seriously negotiating, nor are they shooting at each other. Instead, Iran and the United States have settled into an uneasy, in-between state that risks either a return to fighting or a hardening stalemate. At the core of this unresolved status are calculations, perhaps miscalculations, by each side. Iranian officials believe they have more to gain from withstanding U.S. economic pressure and maintaining control over the Strait of Hormuz than they do from making major concessions in a negotiated deal, analysts said. And the United States appears to be betting that putting Iran in a tighter economic stranglehold will succeed where military strikes have not. On Wednesday, President Trump vowed to impose “tremendous economic consequences” on countries that do business with Iran. So far, neither the U.S. nor Iran has gotten what they want. When the countries agreed to a cease-fire two months ago, it was supposed to put them on a path to a broader deal within 60 days, covering Iran’s nuclear program and the lifting of U.S. sanctions. That deadline passed this week and, on Tuesday, Mr. Trump said on social media that there were “no talks or conversations” going on or scheduled. Instead, the two countries are “in a state of constant limbo,” said Nicole Grajewski, an assistant professor at the Center for International Studies at Sciences Po in Paris. “Not that much has fundamentally changed over the past several months,” she added, “beyond a further entrenchment of the Iranian position and repeated, so far unsuccessful, U.S. efforts to find some kind of way out.” This month, Tehran issued a list of demands on Washington for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which sits along Iran’s southern coast and is a major transit point for much of the world’s oil.
image_caption: A butcher in Tehran in July. The United States appears to be betting that putting Iran in a tighter economic stranglehold will succeed where military strikes have not. Vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, seen from Oman, this week.

headline: Trump’s Overture to Kim Jong-un Strains Alliance With South Korea
article_summary: President Trump wants to curtail military exercises with South Korea, saying they were hostile to North Korea. But under Mr. Kim, the North has become increasingly belligerent toward the South.
article_body: The South Korean and United States militaries view their annual drills in South Korea as more critical than ever. The stakes have risen dramatically as North Korea has gained battlefield expertise with drones and modern warfare by deploying troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine. The summer exercise had barely begun on Monday when President Trump denounced it, dealing yet another blow to the seven-decade-old alliance between Washington and Seoul. Under Mr. Trump, bilateral relations have already come under immense strain from ​his punishing tariffs on South Korean exports.​ And his transactional diplomacy has frustrated South Korea, most recently when he appeared to put Saudi Arabia on the path to enriching nuclear fuel on its own soil, a demand Seoul has made for years. In recent years, North Korea has ​not only expanded its nuclear arsenal but also repeatedly threatened ​to use it against South ​Korea, labeling its neighbor ​a “most ​hostile enemy.” Its leader, Kim Jong-un, has also forged a mutual defense treaty with Moscow, dispatching troops and​ weapons to ​support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Despite these escalations, Mr. Trump, in a social media post , characterized North Korea as “unthreatening and respectful” while boasting of his “very good relationship” with Mr. Kim.​ In the same post, he ​also criticized the decades-old joint military drills with South Korea as “not only costly” but “totally inappropriate and hostile” toward North Korea. “I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea,” he said. “Based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!”
image_caption: U.S. troops at Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek, South Korea, on Monday. The U.S. military’s presence in the country has long acted as a deterrent to North Korea. North Korean soldiers marching during a parade in Moscow in May. The North’s leader, Kim Jong-un, has forged a mutual defense treaty with Russia.

headline: Kushner Meets With Hamas to Advance Trump’s Gaza Plan
article_summary: The president’s son-in-law met the Palestinian militant group’s leaders in Egypt, officials said. He will soon see Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli leader.
article_body: Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and close adviser, met with Hamas leaders in Egypt on Sunday, two Hamas officials and another official briefed on the meetings said. The talks were part of a diplomatic push to advance Mr. Trump’s plan for the future of Gaza. A U.S. official confirmed that Mr. Kushner was in Egypt for talks on Gaza, without providing further details. All four officials spoke on the condition of anonymity to detail Mr. Kushner’s meetings. Mr. Kushner’s visit to the Middle East comes as the U.S.-backed plan to disarm Hamas has appeared to hit a dead end. Last month, Mr. Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached an agreement with Hamas that aimed to strip the Palestinian group of its weapons. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel later said he rejected the deal, appearing to put it on ice. After the meetings with Hamas on Sunday, Mr. Kushner was expected to travel to Israel to meet with Mr. Netanyahu to discuss the situation in Gaza. Direct talks between the U.S. government and Hamas, which the United States has designated as a terrorist organization, were once rare. But the Trump administration broke that taboo, holding multiple rounds of negotiations with the group to win freedom for the hostages Hamas seized in Israel and to end the Israeli military campaign in Gaza. Though Mr. Kushner does not hold an official U.S. government position, Mr. Trump has tapped him, alongside real estate developer Steve Witkoff, to lead diplomacy on matters as diverse as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Israel-Hamas war.
image_caption: Jared Kushner earlier this year.

headline: Liechtenstein Changes Its Law to Allow Women to Ascend the Throne
article_summary: The move puts the principality in the majority among nearby nations with royal families.
article_body: Of the roughly four dozen countries where royal families reign, two have wrestled this summer with questions of gender and succession in the modern era, taking starkly different approaches. Liechtenstein, a tiny nation of about 40,000 people wedged between Switzerland and Austria in the Alps, took one route: On Saturday, it announced that women would now be able to become the monarch and wield the broad political power of the throne. The Princely House of Liechtenstein said in a statement that it was shifting from male-only succession to absolute primogeniture, making the future firstborn child of the ruling royal family heir to the throne, regardless of gender. “With this legislative amendment, we wish to ensure that both the Principality of Liechtenstein and the Princely House are governed by the person best prepared for this task,” said Hereditary Prince Alois, the country’s de facto leader. The sons and daughters of the reigning royal “are familiarized from their youth with the unique characteristics of the Principality and the Princely House,” and will “in principle,” be best suited for the ruling role, he said. Prince Alois, 58, is the son of the reigning Prince Hans-Adam , 81, and he has for more than two decades served as his father’s deputy, handling the duties of head of state in his place. He is a father of four, with an elder son, a daughter and two younger sons, but the rule change does not apply to them or anyone already born. It will apply to all future births, Prince Alois told the local news media. Liechtenstein’s move to adopt equal succession rights puts it in the majority among nearby nations with royal families.
image_caption: Hereditary Prince Alois of Liechtenstein, arriving at the country’s National Day celebrations in Vaduz, the capital, on Saturday.

headline: Iran Says Qatar Captured Its Pilots Months Ago, a Claim Qatar Rejects
article_summary: Iran said the airmen have been held since March 2 when their fighter jets were shot down. The Qatari government denies detaining any Iranian pilots.
article_body: Iran accused Qatar on Saturday of capturing three of its bomber pilots in the early days of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, a claim that a Qatari official publicly denied. Gen. Seyed Mohammad Bagherzadeh, commander of the Iranian armed forces’ missing persons search committee, made the accusation in a letter to the International Committee of the Red Cross, which was published by Iranian media . He said the men were flying Su-24 fighter jets in an operation on March 2, days after the outbreak of the war, when their planes had been hit by “enemy defenses” and the pilots ejected. They survived but were captured by the Qatari authorities, according to General Bagherzadeh, who named the men as Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian. A fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, died, he added. But Majed al-Ansari, a spokesman for Qatar’s foreign ministry, denied that the country had detained the Iranians. “We categorically deny the claims circulating regarding the detention of Iranian pilots & are surprised by these misleading statements at this particular time, amid the ongoing diplomatic efforts & initiatives aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region,” Mr. al-Ansari wrote on social media on Saturday evening. Qatar, a close U.S. ally that hosts a major American military base, said in early March that its Air Force had shot down two Iranian Su-24 bomber jets. Mr. al-Ansari said on Saturday that “contact was established with the pilots concerned following their violation of Qatari airspace.” He added, “After following the rules of engagement & attempting to communicate with them without receiving a response, the necessary measures were taken to defend our territory in accordance with international law.” He said that Qatari search and rescue teams searched for the pilots’ remains. Qatar communicated with Iran to turn over the remains of one pilot who was found, presumably a reference to Mr. Kazemi, Mr. al-Ansari said. Qatar also invited an Iranian team to visit and “be briefed on the details of the search & rescue operations in April, but the Iranian side has yet to respond to the invitation,” Mr. al-Ansari said. General Bagherzadeh’s letter was the most precise indication so far of what Iran believes happened to the three pilots. Before Saturday’s letter, Iranian authorities had said the fate of the men was unknown. Qatar “has not allowed the prisoners to meet or speak with their families or with officials handling their cases,” General Bagherzadeh wrote. He called on the Red Cross to meet with the pilots, investigate their condition, and facilitate their release as soon as possible. The Red Cross did not respond to a request for comment.

headline: Irán se prepara para la guerra y para contener la disidencia interna
article_summary: El líder supremo de Irán nombró a líderes militares de línea dura para altos cargos de seguridad. Los analistas dicen que planea mantener a la nación en pie de guerra.
article_body: Después de casi seis meses en la clandestinidad , el líder supremo de Irán, el ayatolá Mojtaba Jameneí, ha mostrado de forma más clara hasta ahora su visión para gobernar el país, al nombrar a una serie de comandantes militares veteranos de línea dura para altos cargos de seguridad. La reestructuración, que tuvo lugar este mes, señala que planea mantener a la nación en pie de guerra, dicen los analistas, lista para una confrontación sin un final definido con Estados Unidos y para contener la disidencia en el país entre los iraníes que sufren el impacto económico del conflicto . Los nombramientos también reflejan a un liderazgo que sigue teniendo problemas para idear una estrategia sostenible para disuadir a Washington, señalaron los analistas, a medida que Teherán busca una manera de poner fin a la guerra sin renunciar a la ventaja estratégica que ha obtenido, sobre todo a través del control sobre el estrecho de Ormuz. Los nuevos líderes de seguridad primero tendrán que navegar por un periodo de limbo en el conflicto. Aunque las escaramuzas a gran escala han disminuido, ni Washington ni Teherán parecen estar listos para hacer concesiones para llegar a un acuerdo sobre el estrecho de Ormuz. Además, un plazo de 60 días para pactar un acuerdo sobre el programa nuclear de Irán expiró el lunes. El estancamiento ha dejado a la región en un estado de incertidumbre que podría estallar de nuevo en una guerra a gran escala en cualquier momento. Entre los nombramientos hechos por el ayatolá Jameneí, Mohsen Rezaei , quien lideró el Cuerpo de la Guardia Revolucionaria Islámica durante la guerra Irán-Irak, fue nombrado jefe del Consejo Supremo de Seguridad Nacional. Y Hossein Taeb, un clérigo y exjefe de inteligencia, fue elegido para dirigir a los Basij, una poderosa red de fuerzas paramilitares a menudo utilizada para reprimir protestas.
image_caption: Una manifestación en Teherán en abril, con carteles del ayatolá Mojtaba Jameneí. El ayatolá no ha sido visto en público desde que fue nombrado líder supremo de Irán.

headline: Barred From Ballot, a Party Becomes a Vessel for Russians’ Discontent
article_summary: The spotlight on the country’s only antiwar party has brought a spark to what had looked like another dull, tightly controlled election campaign.
article_body: As Nikolai Rybakov, the leader of Russia’s only antiwar party, walked through central Moscow, the growing sentiment against the conflict in Ukraine was easy to see. While I tried to interview him on his way to a subway station, he was constantly approached by passers-by requesting selfies and asking questions. “Are you really against the war?” one young person asked him. “Are you seriously against blockages?” another asked, referring to the Kremlin’s wartime bans or restrictions on popular apps such as Facebook and Telegram. He added: “Are you really going to take the metro? Wow!” It was Friday, and Mr. Rybakov had just filed an appeal of a court decision to remove his party, Yabloko, from the ballot for next month’s parliamentary elections — a decision that the country’s Supreme Court would go on to uphold on Monday. The same fate has befallen other opposition parties during Vladimir V. Putin’s presidency. Yabloko’s last-minute disqualification suggested that the Kremlin had belatedly realized not only how unpopular the war was but also that the party could become a vessel for that discontent. A recent poll found that Russians wanting peace negotiations outnumbered those who favor continued fighting by more than two to one. Mr. Rybakov said the reason for the party’s newfound popularity was people’s growing fatigue with what looked like an endless and fruitless war. Yabloko, he said, “has always been a party that opposes violent action.”
image_caption: Nikolai Rybakov during an appeal of his party’s disqualification before the Russian Supreme Court on Monday.

headline: EE. UU. e Irán incumplen el plazo para lograr un acuerdo de paz
article_summary: El presidente Trump dijo que el alto al fuego de junio pondría límites al programa nuclear de Irán y daría fin al conflicto, pero los países parecen estar muy distanciados.
article_body: El lunes, Estados Unidos e Irán incumplieron su plazo de 60 días para llegar a un acuerdo que limite el programa nuclear iraní bajo los términos del alto al fuego acordado en junio. La falta de un acuerdo subraya la ruptura de una tregua que el presidente Donald Trump prometió que pondría fin a la guerra. Trump había anunciado el llamado memorando de entendimiento entre los dos países con bombos y platillos hace dos meses. Pero el efímero acuerdo no logró reabrir el estrecho de Ormuz, que Irán bloqueó en la práctica luego de que Israel y Estados Unidos atacaran a fines de febrero, ni poner fin a un conflicto que ha entrado en su sexto mes. El vencimiento del plazo es en gran medida simbólico, ya que tanto Trump como los líderes de Irán han dicho en semanas recientes que el acuerdo está básicamente muerto. El acuerdo original también estipulaba que el periodo de 60 días se extendería de ser necesario, lo cual habría sido probable dada la naturaleza delicada y compleja de las negociaciones. Pero el hito, no obstante, demuestra lo mucho que a Trump le ha costado alcanzar sus objetivos de guerra —como obligar a Irán a limitar sus ambiciones nucleares— y lo envalentonado que se siente el gobierno iraní, en un momento en el que ambos países están en riesgo de un conflicto militar más grande. El presidente Trump dijo el lunes que evitar que Irán obtenga un arma nuclear seguía siendo su principal objetivo. “La meta número uno es, y siempre será, que Irán no pueda tener, de ninguna manera, forma o modo, un arma nuclear”, dijo en las redes sociales. Esmail Baghaei, portavoz del Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores iraní, dijo a los periodistas el lunes que las negociaciones sobre el acuerdo nuclear “nunca comenzaron”, y agregó que el periodo de 60 días “en el fondo ya no es relevante”.
image_caption: Transeúntes en Teherán, Irán, el mes pasado. Los iraníes lidian con graves presiones económicas tras seis meses de guerra.

headline: No Way Out
article_summary: The U.S. is building an archipelago of overseas detention sites where deportees are often held indefinitely without charge.
article_body: Donald Trump won election promising to deport millions of immigrants. Many dismissed that as campaign talk. But 19 months after taking office, the administration is as determined as ever to reach its targets. Federal immigration agents have been arresting roughly 2,000 people a day. (Last week we also learned about a plan for ICE agents to get gloves that can deliver electric shocks.) Billions are being spent on new detention centers. And around the world, the U.S. is paying developing countries, from El Salvador to Rwanda, to take deportees off its hands. Today, my colleague Nicholas Casey writes about how America is creating a system of indefinite detention abroad.

headline: A Mother’s Quest to Rescue Her Son From Russian-Occupied Ukraine A Mother’s Quest to Rescue Her Son From Russian-Occupied Ukraine
article_body: A mother of three sat in a Ukrainian rehabilitation center, clutching her phone, willing it to ring, trying to piece her shattered family back together. Liliia Prutian, 55, was working as a military medic when Russian troops invaded in February 2022. They captured her, abused her, accused her of terrorism and held her for two and a half years. After her release, she spent much of her time in this rehabilitation center, in a forest on the outskirts of Kyiv, going to government interviews, doctors’ appointments, group therapy sessions, horseback-riding and ski lessons, massages, yoga classes and reconstructive surgery on her right eardrum. But what Ms. Prutian really wanted was to recover her youngest son, Dima Zahrebaiev, whom she had not seen in three years. He was now 20, living alone in their home in the family village, under Russian occupation since 2022. Fearing he would be forced into the Russian Army, she was desperate to rescue him, though it would be an elaborate, dangerous venture. Finally, just before 7 p.m. one Sunday, the phone jangled and she answered before the first ring finished. Struggling to keep her voice steady, she used bland language, unsure who was listening. “Dima, hey, how are you?” she asked. “Everything OK?” Their separation is the story of many families in the 20 percent of Ukraine controlled by Russia. Millions fled those occupied territories but millions stayed, unwilling or unable to leave. As cities were reduced to rubble, families like Ms. Prutian’s were split, an enduring source of anguish and one reason that Ukraine is balking at giving up land as part of any peace talks. The father of Ms. Prutian’s three sons died years ago. Her oldest son served in the Ukrainian Army. Her middle son joined the Russian Army, leaving Dima, by far the youngest, to fend for himself. She planned Dima’s escape with care, paying a taxi driver about $115 to smuggle him a temporary Ukrainian passport. She hired another driver who ferried people from the occupied territories through Russia to Belarus and eventually back to Ukrainian-controlled territory. On the phone, Ms. Prutian peppered Dima with questions: Was he getting ready to leave? (Yes.) Did he find a hose to drain the heating system? (Yes.) Had he seen his uncle? (Not yet.) Was everything on track as planned? (Yes.) “Make sure to dress warmly for the trip,” she told him. “But don’t overdo it, either. If it gets too warm, you can always take off your jacket. Just don’t let yourself freeze. You might have to wait outside for a long time. Did you decide on shoes? Do you have a pair?” In days, Dima planned to leave the only home he had ever known to meet his mother in Kyiv, where he had never been. He packed a large gym bag, folding up two of his mother’s favorite dresses — one pink, one blue — and some of his T-shirts and sweaters. He stuffed in his soccer ball and his hat. Dima hid his temporary passport inside his backpack. And he waited. Ms. Prutian raised her sons in the cinder-block house her parents had built in Blyzhnie, a village in the Donetsk region of about 750 people, with grain elevators, farms and low-slung buildings. In 2014, protesters ousted the pro-Russian president of Ukraine, and Moscow retaliated by launching a shadow war in eastern Ukraine. The Kremlin backed separatist militias and deployed its own forces in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, the area called the Donbas. Jobs became scarce. Ms. Prutian, who had trained as an accountant, got government aid and earned the equivalent of about $140 a month working at a gas station. Then she decided to join the army, where the pay was about $365 a month. At that time, joining the Ukrainian military was a patriotic statement in the Donbas, where some people sympathized with Russia, pitting neighbor against neighbor, brother against brother. Yet doing so was very rare for a mother. Still, Ms. Prutian was staunchly Ukrainian, and she needed the money, so she enlisted in early 2017, as an accountant for the military, helping to manage the finances of a battalion. The job required her to leave home. She was 47. Her two older sons were adults. Dima was only 12. Ms. Prutian relied on her older sons, relatives and friends to care for Dima. She came back every two or three weeks, and baked honey cakes and made pizzas piled with meat. She rationalized her absences, telling herself she did what a man would do so her family could survive. And, she said, she found a sense of purpose in the army. She trained as a combat medic and, in 2019, was sent to the front lines. When her contract finished, she returned home for five months in 2020 to be with Dima. Then she enlisted again. So did her oldest son. After the full-scale Russian invasion, Ms. Prutian’s unit was sent to protect Mariupol, a vital port city. The battles there were fierce , and the unit kept fighting. Just 16 days into the war, Russian troops surrounded Ms. Prutian and six other Ukrainian soldiers in a village north of Mariupol. Out of ammunition, they surrendered. Three Russians separated her from the men and locked her in a house, interrogating her for days. Why did she join the army? Who did she serve with? The soldiers then demanded sex, she said. Ms. Prutian negotiated. “At least let it be just one of you,” she later recalled saying. One Russian soldier then raped her, she said. The New York Times could not independently verify her account, but it is consistent with those that other women have given to human rights groups of sexual assault in captivity. Russia’s defense ministry did not respond to an inquiry about her experience, but it has generally denied abusing prisoners. Days later, she was locked in a basement cell in Donetsk city. More than 20 women were crammed into a space designed for 10, she said. They had to share mattresses at night, sing the Russian national anthem every morning and stand all day. If they sat down, she said, the guards beat them. Water was scarce, and the toilet stopped working. The women kept leftover soup to use the liquid to flush the toilet, she said. Ms. Prutian’s ears, damaged in combat, became infected. She started losing her hearing. In summer 2023, she was moved to a prison in southern Russia and put on trial on terrorism charges, a case that was covered by local media. At one hearing, her middle son submitted written testimony against her. That was how she learned that he had joined the Russian Army, that their family could never be whole again. Eventually she managed to send letters to Dima and her oldest son. In September 2024, Ms. Prutian was still on trial when she was suddenly released in a prisoner swap. Back on Ukrainian-controlled soil, she kissed the trees and walked barefoot in the grass. Mostly, she worried about Dima. In February 2022, Blyzhnie was a hiccup on the Russian march to the coast. Soldiers overran the village and made it theirs. Ukrainian flags were thrown away or laid on the ground as crude welcome mats in front of grocery stores. Flags went up for the Donetsk People’s Republic, the Russian proxy regime. Troops moved into the homes of residents who had fled, using Blyzhnie as a staging area for assaults on Volnovakha, a nearby transportation hub. At first, Dima, a slight 17-year-old with dark hair, was afraid to step outside. Before her capture, his mother called and texted when possible. Once, he told her he could see Russian soldiers near her fruit trees. Then she stopped responding. For months, he did not know if she was alive. After staying briefly with his middle brother — who had always opposed his mother and older brother joining the Ukrainian Army — Dima moved back home, alone again. Dima, who has Type 1 diabetes, was small for his age, but he had grown up quicker than his friends. He left school after ninth grade, enrolling in a nearby forestry technical college and studying to repair tractors. Now, school had stopped. Jobs were nonexistent. Internet and phone service were frustratingly slow. Walking around Blyzhnie, he put his head down when he passed Russian soldiers. Dima asked his oldest brother, fighting for Ukraine, to send him money, about $80 at a time, which Dima had to convert into Russian rubles to buy groceries. He made simple dishes: pasta, porridge and fried eggs. In September 2022, he got seriously ill from complications from diabetes. His middle brother drove him to the region’s major hospital and left him there. Lying in the intensive care unit, Dima had no idea that his mother was being held prisoner less than five miles away. It was around that time, apparently, that the middle brother definitively chose sides, his mother and brothers said. He married a pro-Russian Ukrainian. He sold his mother’s car. He stopped talking to his brothers. Before long, he enlisted in the Russian Army. It was the kind of rupture that has torn apart families throughout the occupied territories. In the hospital, no one visited Dima. With no adult to take responsibility, he stayed for months until a teacher from his school found him and signed him out. It was winter of 2023, a year after the invasion. More than half of Blyzhnie’s population had fled. Dima found Russian soldiers living in his home but moved back in anyway, a singular protest. The soldiers soon left, abandoning their uneaten military meals, old kettles and an electric stove. Dima noticed many things were missing: cutlery, gold, jewelry, a laptop, and some of his clothes and shoes. He returned to school and took on a part-time construction job. He learned to make borscht and fry sausages. He got a Russian passport, which he needed to pay his utilities, collect canned food from aid agencies and attend school. The war was close. Dima saw dead bodies twice. He saw Russian soldiers and hoped they wouldn’t force him into the army. And he waited. In late February 2025, Dima began his journey. A taxi took him to meet a jeep in Volnovakha, joining others escaping the occupation. One passenger was going to Belarus; another was taking her child to unoccupied Ukraine. Dima lied at border checkpoints. They crossed first into Russia, the only practical and somewhat safe way out of occupied Ukraine, then into Belarus and then Poland before going back to Ukraine, a trip covering 1,740 miles. They slept in the vehicle. When Dima finally arrived in Kyiv and spotted his mother at the train station, he ran to her and hugged her tightly. Ms. Prutian kissed her boy, in his filthy coat and faded jeans. She saw how he smiled but seemed pensive. She felt oddly numb. “I was afraid that I didn’t feel anything,” she later explained. “I can’t say I felt joy. Meeting him felt like meeting a stranger. They say that’s normal after captivity.” Ms. Prutian set up a new home with Dima and her older son, now discharged from the military, in Dnipro, a city about 60 miles west of the frontline. People back home said her middle son had suffered a head injury in a drone attack. She didn’t try to find out more. Ms. Prutian dreams of returning to their village. For now, she has a desk job in the Ukrainian Army. It takes her away from home much of the time, but it is far from the fighting. Adjustment to life with her sons has been hard — they had to work to fit back together. Dima was initially so reserved that he asked permission for everything, and did not talk much. “Dima, don’t be afraid,” his mother told him. “No one here’s going to punish you for what you say.” Slowly, he opened up, taking his mother’s hand when they walked, as he used to. He resumed taking classes. Lately, Ms. Prutian has started feeling like herself again. Still, she treats Dima as if he were much younger. She constantly mothers him, wiping his face, hugging him. “Maybe I feel guilty for not doing enough when I couldn’t, but I don’t feel I’m overdoing it now,” she said. “You can never love someone too much.”
