headline: 5 Americans Are Killed in Helicopter Crash in Kenya
article_summary: Ecuador’s director of national intelligence was also among those who died in the crash. The search and recovery efforts were being hampered by a fire at the site and the difficult terrain, officials said.
article_body: A helicopter crashed on Wednesday at a tourist destination in northern Kenya, killing at least five Americans and a senior government official from Ecuador, the authorities said. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority said the crash happened about 9 a.m. at Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County, a rural and arid area that attracts tourists to its national park and wildlife conservancies. The crash occurred as the helicopter, a Eurocopter, was flying to Ewaso Nyiro River, the site of several upmarket wildlife tourist camps, the aviation authority said. “We confirm the deaths of five Americans,” a U.S. State Department spokesperson said in a statement, which gave no details about the identities of the victims. But among the other victims were Michele Sensi-Contugi, Ecuador’s intelligence chief, 44, and his wife, Stephany Hollihan, a 43-year-old fashion designer, according to Ecuador’s government. The death of Mr. Sensi-Contugi, one of President Daniel Noboa’s closest and most strategically important officials, comes at a critical time for Ecuador. Intelligence has become central to the country’s response to an extraordinary crisis of drug violence and crime , and to its increasingly close security relationship with the United States.
image_caption: A photograph released by the Kenya Red Cross showing emergency response teams during a search and rescue operation after the helicopter crash near Mount Ololokwe in Samburu, Kenya, on Wednesday.

headline: Carney and Trump Talk Again as Deadline Nears on New U.S. Tariffs
article_summary: Canada is seeking a deal to dodge further economic pain at the hands of the Trump administration on midnight Tuesday. But at what cost?
article_body: Canada is bracing for a U.S. tariff deadline arriving at midnight on Tuesday, when a number of new levies by the Trump administration will come into effect unless negotiators strike an 11th-hour deal. President Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada spoke on Tuesday afternoon, the prime minister’s office said. The call was related to trade and no other details were given. A proposal of terms hammered out over the past few days by negotiators from both sides was handed to Mr. Trump on Tuesday afternoon, a United States official said. At the heart of the talks is how many concessions Canada is prepared to make to secure not just a cancellation of the proposed tariffs but also an improvement of those already in place — and whether the Trump administration is prepared to budge. The United States’ trade representative, Jamieson Greer, who is heading the talks for the U.S. side, said last week that he expected Canada to drop certain measures it had already taken in response to U.S. tariffs. “If a country retaliates against us, we’re obviously not going to tolerate that,” Mr. Greer told reporters in Iowa on Friday. “We’ll take action. My sense is the Canadians want to have a more conciliatory approach, but we’ll see.”
image_caption: The Gordie Howe International Bridge, connecting Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, on the day after it opened last month. President Trump had threatened to block the bridge’s opening.

headline: Thieves Steal 4 Renaissance Paintings From Italian Museum in Brazen Heist
article_summary: The works, by Antonello da Messina, were taken as the Sicilian city of Messina held a religious celebration.
article_body: Four paintings by the Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Messina, Sicily, on Saturday, Italian officials said. Taking advantage of an annual religious celebration that brings tens of thousands to Messina’s streets, thieves made off with three of five panels that constitute the Polyptych of San Gregorio as well as a small double-sided devotional painting . They are the only works by Antonello da Messina, commonly called Antonello, that remained in his native city. The celebration, the Procession of the Vara, is a religious ritual that takes places every Aug. 15. Some 100,000 people attended the celebration and the city’s law enforcement officials were focused on maintaining order there, city officials said. “Coinciding with la Vara, it was certainly a planned theft,” Mayor Federico Basile said in a telephone interview. Commissioned in the 15th century for the church of San Gregorio, which was destroyed during a devastating earthquake in 1908 , the San Gregorio altarpiece originally consisted of six panels. Only five remain and were housed at Messina’s Accascina Regional Museum. The thieves initially took all five remaining panels, but left two behind near a fence outside the museum, perhaps in their haste to escape, Mr. Basile said. The mayor said that passers-by noticed “suspicious activity” at the museum and immediately alerted the police. Vincenzo Caruso, Messina’s chief cultural official, said that the thieves smashed a sealed case to get to the other work they stole, a small double-sided panel that depicts the Madonna and Child with a Franciscan friar on one side, and Christ on the other.
image_caption: The five surviving panels of Antonello da Messina’s 1473 “San Gregorio Polyptych,” three of which were stolen from the Accascina Regional Museum in Messina, Italy.

headline: Fueron amigas de la infancia. Luego, descubrieron que eran hermanas
article_summary: Meena Geltink y Minal Tijssen fueron adoptadas en India por familias de los Países Bajos y crecieron a menos de 160 kilómetros de distancia.
article_body: Una noche de esta primavera, Meena Geltink acostó a su hijo menor y se sentó en el sofá con su pareja, lista para tomar una taza de té. Entonces vio un mensaje en Facebook de una amiga de la infancia que cambiaría su vida. “¿Te acuerdas de mí?”, escribió su amiga, Minal Tijssen. Habían pasado 15 años desde la última vez que se habían visto. Tijssen había incluido una captura de pantalla del sitio web de genealogía MyHeritage y le preguntó si Geltink también había recibido una notificación de ellos. Geltink, quien nació en India y fue adoptada por una familia en los Países Bajos en la década de 1980, había estado buscando a sus familiares biológicos desde 2017, cuando envió una muestra de ADN a MyHeritage. Como habían pasado tantos años sin encontrar una coincidencia, Geltink había borrado la aplicación unos meses antes. Con las manos temblorosas, volvió a instalarla y de inmediato recibió la misma notificación que Tijssen. Ahí estaba: una coincidencia de ADN. Geltink y Tijssen tenían los mismos padres. “Rompí a llorar”, dijo Geltink en una entrevista telefónica. Geltink, de 43 años, y Tijssen, de 44, se habían conocido de adolescentes durante un evento de fin de semana organizado para niños adoptados. Entablaron una amistad al instante. “Vi su nariz, sus ojos: todo se parecía a mí”, dijo Geltink. Al crecer en un pequeño pueblo neerlandés, donde casi todos eran blancos, Geltink dijo que había estado “buscando mi identidad”. Tijssen se crio a menos de 160 kilómetros de distancia. Ambas dijeron que eran unidas a sus familias adoptivas y que habían crecido con un hermano.
image_caption: Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen were born in India and grew up with different adoptive families in the Netherlands. Decades after becoming friends, a DNA test has revealed that the two are also biological sisters.

headline: As Iran War Turns Into Economic Battle, a New U.S. Strategy Recalls Old Ones
article_summary: The United States and Iran are poised to blow past a deadline they had set themselves to broker terms on peace and Iran’s nuclear program.
article_body: President Trump’s cease-fire with Iran in June envisioned a broader deal to end the war and rein in the country’s nuclear program, all negotiated within 60 days. But that deadline, set to pass on Monday, has been essentially abandoned, and the war has transformed into a contest of willpower and economic endurance that has no end in sight. There have been no publicly reported U.S. strikes on Iranian targets since late July. Yet the effective collapse of the agreement underscores how Mr. Trump has struggled to end the war he started in February alongside Israel, and how far he remains from the ambitions of the June deal, including fully reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway where Iran has choked off oil and gas shipping since the fighting began. Those inside the White House are well aware that they will blow past Monday’s deadline and that the conflict has largely morphed into one of economic warfare, according to two Americans familiar with the negotiations. The current strategy bears a striking resemblance to previous, yearslong U.S. attempts to isolate Iran in the hopes of compelling it to abandon its nuclear ambitions. The policy had mixed results, and some analysts are skeptical that even severe economic pressure on its own will force Iran to change course. After all, that was the approach Mr. Trump attempted in his first term, even though his Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said last week that he was about to impose financial penalties unlike any seen before. The June memorandum of understanding was widely seen as a boon for Iran, granting the regime badly needed sanctions relief even as talks over tough concessions like nuclear enrichment were postponed for later. But Iranian leaders opted to escalate again rather than consolidate their gains from the deal, according to Nate Swanson, an Iran expert at the Atlantic Council, a Washington-based research group. Ships could move through the Strait of Hormuz freely before the war. Iran’s insistence that the deal’s vague language on the issue gave it control over the waterway led to the deal falling apart . Iran began firing on ships that transited in channels outside Iranian waters, and American forces retaliated by bombing southern Iran, prompting a cycle of attacks and counterattacks across the Middle East. Now, Iran refuses to reopen the strait until the United States follows through on its commitments from the cease-fire, like releasing frozen Iranian assets abroad. The Trump administration wants Iran to first end the blockade, said Ali Vaez, an Iran expert at the International Crisis Group, a research institute. “Neither side is really ready to finalize a deal. They both think that in a matter of days or weeks, the other side will be more desperate for a deal, so they’ll be able to get more out of it,” Mr. Vaez said. “This is why we are locked into this game of endurance again.” On Saturday, the United Arab Emirates’ foreign ministry slammed Iran for attacking a vessel affiliated with the state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company the previous day. Iranian officials did not comment. Reopening the strait has increasingly become Mr. Trump’s main focus in the conflict, even though he initially said the war was meant to empower the Iranian people to overthrow the existing regime , severely degrade its missile capability and stop Tehran from getting a nuclear weapon. There has been little indication that Iran and the United States have extensively discussed the Iranian nuclear program since the cease-fire in June, let alone formulated a deal that could satisfy both sides. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said over the weekend that Iran had yet to decide whether to resume talks with the United States. But the 60-day timeline was no longer relevant, he added, given that the June agreement was essentially defunct. “We did not have a cease-fire that now needs to be extended,” Mr. Araghchi said. “We had an end to the war, which has now taken on a new status.” Former U.S. officials who worked on Iran say the prospect of a new nuclear deal between the United States and Iran within 60 days was always remote, although the agreement provided for extensions. A previous, Obama-era, agreement took about two years of delicate talks to negotiate. Mr. Trump withdrew from that deal, called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, in 2018. The Trump administration hoped that the June agreement would, at the very least, open the Strait of Hormuz. But to get the deal over the line, they relied on vague language that lent credibility to Iran’s claim to dominate future shipping in the waterway, analysts said. “It was a flawed document; it was hurried out when it wasn’t ready for prime time,” said Mr. Swanson, the Iran expert. “And they didn’t resolve the most important short-term issue, which was the strait.” Instead, the United States and Iran now seem to be settling in for an indefinite struggle, neither at all-out war nor in a defined peace. Seeking to force Iran to accept U.S. terms, the Trump administration has brought back sanctions on Iranian oil and reinstated a naval blockade, both of which were temporarily canceled by the agreement. Iran’s strained economy, which prompted mass protests that were brutally crushed early this year, is a major consideration for Iranian decision makers. But Mr. Swanson argued that the current stalemate was more likely to push Iran toward escalation than toward conciliation. While there has been little progress on the commitments outlined in the agreement, Mr. Trump and his Iranian counterparts have continued to exchange a war of words. During an event in Garden City, N.Y. , on Friday, Mr. Trump appeared once again intent on changing the narrative, saying he would soon be “declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.” It was not clear how serious Mr. Trump’s proposal was. But doing so could involve deploying boots on the ground and almost certainly would require a prolonged Navy presence — moves antithetical to the “America First” values of Trump supporters who want an end to prolonged military conflicts overseas. Mr. Trump has also been known to toss out half-baked ideas on foreign policy to redirect attention and scrutiny, like when he shocked the world last year by proposing a U.S. takeover of the Gaza Strip , an idea that never materialized. The White House on Saturday did not respond to questions over whether the administration had developed actual plans to take control of the Strait of Hormuz. Mr. Trump’s aides also did not respond to questions over the approaching Monday deadline. Iranian officials, in turn, have defied Mr. Trump as they push their own demands — including one that they had not made before war. “Accept reality once and for all. So far, you have suffered major strategic defeats,” Kazem Gharibabadi, the Iranian deputy foreign minister, said on social media. “The Strait of Hormuz has been Iranian, is Iranian, and will remain Iranian.”
image_caption: Ships anchored this month in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. People waiting at a taxi station in April in Tehran, where a mural depicts Iran holding the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump on Friday at a political event in Garden City, N.Y.

headline: Cholera Outbreak Sickens Over 90 in Myanmar’s Biggest City
article_summary: Civil war and military rule have weakened Myanmar’s health care system, while heavy monsoon rains have increased the risk of waterborne disease.
article_body: At least 93 patients have tested positive for cholera at a single hospital in Myanmar’s biggest city, officials said, as an outbreak that began last week spread across the region. They are among more than 180 people in the city, Yangon, who have been hospitalized with diarrhea, a common symptom of the disease, Dr. Nanda Win, the head of the Yangon Region Public Health and Medical Services Department, said Friday. One 92-year-old man had died, he said. The outbreak is the latest strain on Myanmar’s faltering medical system, which has been neglected under a junta rule that has prioritized weapons over health budgets . Dr. Nanda Win said cases were concentrated in downtown Yangon, many of them in Chinatown, and identified contaminated water and takeaway street food as possible sources. Officials are still tracking where patients live and have traveled to determine how widely the disease has spread. The authorities were preparing supplies at 83 other hospitals across the Yangon region and were working to ensure that the water supply was safe, he said. Cholera outbreaks are not unusual in Myanmar, but experts say they are rare in the Yangon region and attribute the latest outbreak to poor sanitation.
image_caption: The emergency department of Yangon General Hospital on Friday.

headline: Trump Orders Pentagon to Curtail Military Exercises With Ally South Korea
article_summary: In a social media post, the president scolded South Korea for not helping denuclearize Iran, and also praised North Korea and its leader.
article_body: President Trump said on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, a longtime U.S. ally and a linchpin of America’s national security strategy in the Asia-Pacific region. The announcement may heighten growing worries among Asian allies over what the United States is now willing to do to deter China, given the enormous distraction and resource drain of the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. The United States is running low on critical weapons and has been moving military resources out of Asia to the Middle East. In a convoluted social media post , Mr. Trump complained that Seoul did not “join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” In the same post, he said that North Korea under Kim Jong Un had been “unthreatening and respectful” while he has been president. In his post Mr. Trump did not mention a rift in relations in 2017, when the North Korean leader called him a “mentally deranged dotard” after Mr. Trump delivered a speech at the U.N. threatening to “totally destroy” North Korea if the United States had to defend itself or its allies. Now Mr. Trump is speaking only of what he on Sunday called his “very good relationship” with North Korea and its leader. In his post, he said that because of those ties, he was “not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military exercises with South Korea.” “These exercises are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!), but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful,” Mr. Trump said in his post.
image_caption: President Trump on Sunday instructed the Pentagon to reduce its joint military exercises with South Korea, a key U.S. ally in Asia. He also touted his good relationship with Kim Jong-un, North Korea’s leader.

headline: Un sacerdote africano llena el vacío que dejó la escasez de curas en la Italia rural Un sacerdote africano llena el vacío que dejó la escasez de curas en la Italia rural
article_body: El sacerdote entró en el dormitorio donde su feligrés de 90 años yacía durmiendo en una cama de hospital, flanqueado por tanques de oxígeno. El cura estaba de pie junto a la cama y se inclinó para acercarse al paciente, Carlo Martini, mientras los ojos del anciano se abrían brevemente. “¿Cómo estás?”, preguntó el sacerdote, el padre Vincent Souly, con un tono un poco alto. La esposa de Martini, Renza Giagnoni, estaba de pie a un lado y observaba. “¡Parece que somos las Naciones Unidas!”, dijo, también con un tono bastante alto. Souly es una de las pocas personas de raza negra en la provincia de Prato, una región montañosa de la Toscana, en el centro de Italia, donde ha sido sacerdote católico durante 15 años. Ha forjado relaciones cordiales con su rebaño, predominantemente italiano, y muchos feligreses lo aceptan con cariño. Souly nació en Burkina Faso, y creció y fue ordenado en Costa de Marfil. Ahora es ciudadano italiano y está decidido a quedarse en Prato mientras se le necesite. Sin embargo, según él, su pasaporte italiano no necesariamente hace que los demás lo vean como italiano. “De donde yo vengo, decimos: ‘Por mucho tiempo que se quede en el agua, un trozo de madera nunca se convertirá en un cocodrilo’”, dijo. “Te aceptan, hasta cierto punto. Pero hay una parte que no se dice, ¿verdad? Sigues siendo lo que eres”. Sintió un destello de esa otredad cuando Giagnoni se refirió a las Naciones Unidas, nos contó más tarde, o cuando los feligreses se referían a él como un “ prete di colore ” o “sacerdote de color”.
image_caption: El reverendo Vincent Souly fuera de una iglesia en Luicciana, en la Toscana. Ha servido durante 15 años como sacerdote católico romano en la región montañosa de Italia.

headline: How Satellite Advances Are Changing the Game for Ukraine How Satellite Advances Are Changing the Game for Ukraine
article_body: The Russian drone pilots had bedded down for the night. Their white vehicle was parked in the driveway of a small house in occupied southern Ukraine. About 30 miles away, two Ukrainian drone pilots had parked their truck in a tree line at the edge of a field and assembled a medium-size drone loaded with two bombs. Their target? The sleeping Russian drone pilots. The Ukrainian team had a powerful new battlefield tool that night: high-tech satellite imagery providing near real-time information on troop movements and locations. A year ago, it could take days for satellite imagery to get to frontline troops, slowed by less sophisticated technology and layers of command structure. That made it difficult to hit targets that can move locations, like troops in a house, with long-range drone strikes. Now, a support team monitoring the house provided the drone operators a fresh satellite image showing the car in the driveway, an indication the Russians were there. “The target is confirmed,” whispered one of the pilots, who identified himself with the call sign Tikhi, in accordance with Ukrainian military protocol. The rapid delivery of high-quality satellite images to frontline troops is one of the key battlefield advancements of the last year, enabling Ukraine to strike quickly against weapons depots, logistical hubs and troop encampments deep within territory held by Russia, and in Russia itself.
image_caption: A Ukrainian soldier preparing a drone for a strike on a Russian target in the Zaporizhzhia region of Ukraine last month.

headline: The Tragic Story of Jason Arday
article_summary: The Cambridge professor, found dead last week, was at the center of a firestorm about race and hiring. We talk to the reporter covering the story.
article_body: If ever a story seemed tailor-made to pour fuel on the culture war fires, it was the tragic story of Jason Arday. The Cambridge professor recently resigned under scrutiny, and was found dead last week in a South London home. His story touches on deeply divisive topics, from race to higher education to D.E.I. to autism. There’s so much to unpack. To make sense of it all, I spoke to my colleague Mara Hvistendahl, who’s been reporting on Arday’s life, his death and the fallout at Cambridge. Three years ago, Jason Arday, then 37, was hired as a professor at Cambridge University. Cambridge made a big deal of its new star, touting him as its youngest Black professor and promoting his incredible personal story of growing up in public housing and overcoming severe developmental delays to go on to academia. Then, last month, a blog post — written by a former Cambridge researcher once disciplined after arguing Black people couldn’t succeed in a meritocracy — accused Arday of plagiarism and embellishing his life story. A firestorm ensued. British media, especially British conservative media, found the story irresistible. Eventually, Arday resigned, saying he no longer wished to feel as if he was “living under a constant spotlight.” Last week, he was found dead in a London apartment; in a statement, his family referenced the “campaign of sustained abuse” he’d endured.

headline: Six Years in Provence: An Ancient Castle and a Feud Over a Troublesome Bridge
article_summary: In a picturesque village, the mayor closed a road, setting off a storm with residents and the owners of a castle that once belonged to his family.
article_body: In Ansouis, a camera-ready French Provençal village crowned by a majestic medieval castle, the residents insist they are tired of talking about the bridge. And yet the bridge is the only thing anyone seems to talk about. A modest arched span with moss-covered stones, it paralyzes their traffic. It disrupts their routines. It threatens their livelihoods. It is, in the words of a newsletter published by the mayor’s office, “a bridge too far.” On June 4, the mayor, Géraud de Sabran-Pontevès, blocked a main road that runs under the bridge, which is about 22 feet tall, citing danger from structural weaknesses in the arch. The closure effectively cut Ansouis in two, making it impossible to drive through without an exasperating back-street detour. It’s the third time in six years that the mayor has taken this extraordinary step, each time at the height of the summer tourist season. Local merchants say the closures deprive them of valuable traffic because Google Maps and other apps warn motorists about the disruption. Each time, the mayor has cited safety concerns. “I take the risk of a stone falling on someone’s head,” Mr. de Sabran-Pontevès said in an interview, adding that regional authorities had ordered him to close the road.
image_caption: The closure of a main road under a bridge in Ansouis, France, has pitted the mayor against the owners of a castle who rely on the bridge to reach their home. Géraud de Sabran-Pontevès, the mayor of Ansouis, in his study. He blocked the road in June, citing structural weaknesses in its arch.

headline: How Israel’s Financial Chokehold Is Stifling the West Bank Economy
article_summary: Intensifying restrictions have hit every part of the territory’s dealings, spurring worries about whether the Palestinian Authority can remain solvent.
article_body: Israeli pressure on the West Bank has sent the occupied territory to the brink of financial collapse as severe restrictions have touched every part of daily life and caused an economic crisis. Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has stopped thousands of Palestinians from working in Israel, withheld billions of dollars of tax revenues and enforced banking restrictions that have harmed business. The Palestinian Authority, which administers parts of the West Bank, has been forced to cut spending on salaries and public services because of the sharp fall in revenues. The reductions have been felt acutely in sectors such as health care, with pharmacies routinely running out of medicines as the government allocates less money to buy them. The budget cuts have also forced clinics to open only a few days a week and hospitals to operate with fewer doctors and nurses. Ibtisam Hammad, 54, was diagnosed with breast cancer three months ago. After a hospital appointment in the West Bank city of Ramallah, she made her way to a pharmacy to collect her medications. Only three of her six prescriptions were in stock. “I’m lucky,” Ms. Hammad said, smiling despite her exhaustion. “Last time, they only had one.” Ms. Hammad’s trouble getting medicines was indicative of wider economic problems. The Palestinian Authority has often warned of a financial collapse that never materialized, but there are growing concerns about how long it can remain solvent. “We’re facing a huge problem,” Mohammed Mustafa, the authority’s prime minister, said in an interview. “Everyone has been affected.”
image_caption: Montaser Amro, left, and his brother inspecting a box of unpaid bills at his supermarket in Majd, West Bank. Mr. Amro said that his customers owed him around $155,000 and that he was struggling to pay suppliers.

headline: Kushner Meets Netanyahu in Effort to Break Logjam Over Gaza
article_summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel has refused to pull back the country’s military until Hamas fully disarms. But the Trump administration is under pressure to show progress.
article_body: Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and senior aide, met for several hours with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in Jerusalem on Monday in an effort to break a logjam over Mr. Trump’s plan for the future of the war-ravaged Gaza Strip. Mr. Kushner traveled to the region with representatives of Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace after Mr. Netanyahu rejected a deal for Hamas to disarm. A 15-point “road map” that Hamas agreed with the Board of Peace called for the militant group to lay down its weapons and for Israeli forces to withdraw from Gaza. Mr. Trump’s announcement last month that the Board of Peace had secured Hamas’s agreement to disarm briefly raised hopes for progress. The president’s plan had been stalled for months over Hamas’s resistance to disarming and Israel’s continuing airstrikes and military operations in Gaza. Israel has also failed to meet its commitments to allow specified amounts of fuel and other necessities into the territory under the terms of a cease-fire agreed with Hamas in October 2025. It was not clear how much progress had been made in the meetings on Monday. Mr. Netanyahu’s office said in an English-language statement that the two sides had “deep and constructive” discussions and agreed to set up working groups on disarming militant factions in Gaza and the demilitarization of the territory, as well as on sanitation, clean water and other public health issues. Israel and the Board of Peace, the prime minister’s office added, were “determined” that disarmament and demilitarization precede any reconstruction of Gaza, where cities and towns remain in ruins and many people live in dilapidated tents. A Board of Peace official, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, said it had agreed there would be no Israeli “redeployment” from Gaza before disarmament and demilitarization. Israel, the official said, has the right of self-defense if Hamas resorts to violence or attempts to rearm.
image_caption: Jared Kushner speaking about the Board of Peace, an organization backed by the Trump administration to end the war in Gaza, during the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January.

headline: ‘Posh George,’ the Convicted Fraudster in Nigel Farage’s Inner Circle
article_summary: George Cottrell’s close alliance with Mr. Farage is back in the spotlight now that the Reform U.K. leader has returned to Parliament.
article_body: Before George Cottrell became famous in Britain as “Posh George,” a near-constant sidekick to the right wing politician Nigel Farage, he traveled to Las Vegas to meet with drug traffickers for whom he’d offered to launder money. It was 2014, and Mr. Cottrell was 21. He had met the traffickers on the dark web. Under the pseudonym “Bill,” he said he would take $20,000, send it to offshore accounts, and return it clean. Later, according to a federal indictment filed in 2016, he threatened to extort the traffickers for the Bitcoin equivalent of $80,000. It was not until Mr. Cottrell was arrested at O’Hare International Airport in Chicago two years later that it became clear the drug dealers he had met in Las Vegas were actually I.R.S. agents conducting a sting. On July 22, 2016, he and Mr. Farage were heading back to London after a whirlwind week at the Republican National Convention — where Mr. Farage was lauded for his role in Britain’s recent Brexit vote — when five agents detained Mr. Cottrell as he came off a connecting flight. For many high-profile political figures, an aide pleading guilty to wire fraud and serving an eight-month prison sentence might have been enough to end ties. Not so for Mr. Farage, a maverick politician and ally of President Trump who worked for two decades to engineer Britain’s departure from the European Union and who now leads Reform U.K., an anti-immigration party that has outpolled the Conservative Party for 18 months. Mr. Cottrell, 32, has remained among Mr. Farage’s closest advisers. In 2017 he told The Telegraph that he saw him as a father figure and in an interview with Tatler in 2024 he jokingly referred to him as “Daddy.” The bond between the two men has become the subject of intense interest in Britain in recent weeks, following revelations in The Sunday Times of London that Mr. Cottrell provided Mr. Farage with undisclosed gifts and support before the 2024 general election. The police are separately investigating the legality of two donations to Reform of 250,000 pounds each from Mr. Cottrell’s mother, Fiona, and said last month that they had questioned two people, although no arrests have been made.
image_caption: Nigel Farage and George Cottrell in Brussels in 2020, as the European Parliament ratified the terms of Brexit, which both men campaigned for.

headline: A Consulate Shooting, a Toronto Street and a Network of Guns for Hire A Consulate Shooting, a Toronto Street and a Network of Guns for Hire
article_body: The apartment towers on Martha Eaton Way loom over an urban creek in north Toronto, a working-class part of the city where ethnic stores dominate the strip malls. Violent episodes have cast a long shadow over the neighborhood, known as “Creek” to the young people for whom the address can confer clout. Some remember that an 8-year-old boy was killed by a stray bullet through his bedroom window last summer, and that a teenager was fatally shot at the pizza shop next door a year before that. Others are too young to know that an adjacent street is named after a Toronto police officer killed there decades ago, or that a gang from this neighborhood played a defining role in the city’s bloody “summer of the gun” in 2005 . Crime is broadly low in Toronto, with homicides and car theft rates dropping over the last year. But a recent spate of shootings has put many on edge, including synagogues and Jewish schools and storefronts that have been targeted by gunfire. Then, in March, two gunmen fired at the U.S. Consulate in the heart of Toronto’s downtown; a stark, low-rise structure on a busy avenue dotted with court offices, university buildings and hospitals. Security cameras showed the gunmen taking turns to fire the same weapon at the building. Hunting for them, investigators zeroed in on the three apartment towers on Martha Eaton Way. Their investigation took a tragic turn in June, when a police officer trying to carry out a search warrant inside one of the buildings was shot dead.
image_caption: Outside Martha Eaton Way in Toronto.

headline: With Priests Scarce in Rural Italy, an African Pastor Is Filling the Void With Priests Scarce in Rural Italy, an African Pastor Is Filling the Void
article_body: The priest stepped into the bedroom where his 90-year-old parishioner lay sleeping in a hospital bed, flanked by oxygen tanks. The pastor towered over the bed and leaned down to move close to the patient, Carlo Martini, as the old man’s eyes fluttered open briefly. “How are you?” the priest, the Rev. Vincent Souly, asked, a bit too loudly. Mr. Martini’s wife, Renza Giagnoni, stood to the side and watched. “It looks like we’re the United Nations!” she said, also a bit too loudly. Father Souly is one of the few Black faces in the province of Prato, a mountainous region of Tuscany, in central Italy, where he has served for 15 years as a Roman Catholic priest. He has built warm relationships with his predominantly Italian flocks and is embraced by many parishioners. Born in Burkina Faso, and raised and ordained in the Ivory Coast, he is now an Italian citizen and is committed to staying in Prato as long as he is needed. Yet, he said, his Italian passport does not necessarily make others see him as Italian. “Where I’m from, we say, ‘A piece of wood, no matter how long it stays in water, will never become a crocodile,’” he said. “You’re accepted, up to a point. But there’s this unspoken part, right? You remain what you are.” He felt a flash of that otherness when Ms. Giagnoni referred to the United Nations, he told us later, or when parishioners referred to him as a “prete di colore” or “priest of color.” He would prefer that people refer to him by his country of origin rather than by the color of his skin, he said. “When you say, ‘He is an African priest,’ it’s already more elegant, it’s more cultured,” he said. “That means that you’ve tried to locate where Africa is on the world map. If you say, ‘He is from the Ivory Coast,’ that’s even better. Using the color is a shortcut.”
image_caption: The Rev. Vincent Souly outside a church in Luicciana, in Tuscany. He has served for 15 years as a Roman Catholic priest in the mountainous region of Italy.

headline: Houthis Claim Strike on Saudi Vessel as Red Sea Violence Escalates
article_summary: The armed group, based in Yemen and backed by Iran, said it had launched missiles near the vital maritime trade route, in a conflict that shows no sign of abating.
article_body: Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militants said on Monday that they had launched a missile attack on a Saudi ship in the Red Sea, the latest strike in an escalating conflict near one of the world’s most critical trade routes. A spokesman for the Houthi militia, Yahya Saree, said on social media that the group had struck a Saudi military ship and four escort vessels. He added that the group was “closely monitoring” Saudi military movements in Yemen and that it would target Saudi forces “on land and at sea.” The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Houthi claims. But the armed forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which depends on Saudi Arabia military and financially, said on social media that the targeted vessel was a commercial ship that had been out of service since last year. The ship was in the Yemeni port of Mokha, an ancient trading city that has become a frontline site as fighting has reignited in recent weeks. Houthi drone and missile bombardments have halted commercial operations at the port, severing a crucial lifeline for incoming aid and supplies. The attack on Monday took place near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, a narrow maritime choke point at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. The waterway is vital for global commerce, connecting Asia to Europe and the Mediterranean Sea via the Suez Canal. The strait has become especially important for Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February and the Iranian authorities effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz. The Saudi authorities turned to the Red Sea as an alternative route for exporting oil, but the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi vessels last month, and have repeatedly fired on Saudi-linked vessels. A Houthi attack last week killed at least six people on a cargo vessel , according to the Yemeni government. These were the first-known fatalities in the Red Sea from Houthi fire since the start of the war with Iran. The renewed fighting threatens to unravel a fragile calm in Yemen established by a 2022 United Nations-brokered truce . In 2014, the Houthis drove Yemen’s internationally recognized government out of the capital, Sanaa. A year later, a Saudi-led military coalition intervened to restore the government, plunging the impoverished nation into a devastating decade-long war. Yemeni government officials have often accused the Houthis of using the country’s position along global trade routes as leverage in a broader proxy battle.
image_caption: Flames and smoke rising from the port of Mokha in Yemen on Friday. The Houthis have bombarded the city with drones and missiles n recent weeks.

headline: How a Ukrainian Bank Worker Came to Face Life in a Russian Prison
article_summary: Artem Murdid, his mother and his girlfriend are accused of terrorism. They say they did nothing wrong.
article_body: Russia says Artem Murdid is a killer who followed orders from Ukrainian intelligence to plant bombs in his Ukrainian city, Melitopol, after Russian troops captured it. Mr. Murdid says he did nothing wrong. He also says that after he was arrested in March 2023, pro-Russian guards repeatedly beat him, shocked him with electric charges and forced him to watch his mother be subjected to the same. In a letter detailing what he says happened, Mr. Murdid, 32, wrote that the guards also threatened to throw his mother and girlfriend into a trench “where they’ll be raped, while you watch all of this.” He said the guards then threatened to shoot him and leave him along a road for dogs to eat. The Russian authorities did not respond to a request for comment on Mr. Murdid’s claims. Eventually, he wrote, he signed confession papers that were put in front of him, without reading them. So did his mother, Hanna Murdid, 52, and his girlfriend, Hanna Voshkoder, 29. He was given a life sentence, his mother 22 years in prison and his girlfriend 20 years. They were all accused of being part of a terrorist cell. “A lot of people break. I know quite a few people who have been through Russian prisons in recent years,” said Yaroslav Bevza, a close friend of the Murdid family who fled Melitopol after the Russians invaded Ukraine in February 2022. “People would confess to killing Kennedy.” The sentences given to Mr. Murdid, his mother and his girlfriend are on the extreme end of what human rights experts and Ukrainian government officials describe as a black hole for Ukrainian civilians in Russian custody, which they say number in the thousands.
image_caption: Artem Murdid during a trip with friends to a beach on the Sea of Azov in the Zaporizhzhia region in 2019. He says he was tortured into confessing to Russian terrorism charges.

headline: ‘Everything Looked Like Me’: Adopted Childhood Friends Discover They’re Sisters
article_summary: Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen were adopted from India by families in the Netherlands and grew up less than 100 miles apart.
article_body: One evening this spring, Meena Geltink put her youngest child to bed and sat down on the couch with her partner, ready to have a cup of tea. Then she saw a Facebook message from a childhood friend that would change her life. “Do you remember me?” wrote the friend, Minal Tijssen. It had been 15 years since the two had seen each other. Ms. Tijssen had included a screenshot from the genealogy website MyHeritage and asked whether Ms. Geltink had also received a notification from them. Ms. Geltink, who was born in India and adopted by a family in the Netherlands in the 1980s, had been searching for biological family members since 2017, when she sent a DNA sample to MyHeritage. Because so many years had passed without a match, Ms. Geltink had deleted the app a few months earlier. With shaking hands, she reinstalled it and promptly received the same notification as Ms. Tijssen. There it was: a DNA match. Ms. Geltink and Ms. Tijssen had the same parents. “I burst into tears,” Ms. Geltink said in a phone interview. Ms. Geltink, 43, and Ms. Tijssen, 44, had first met as teenagers during an organized weekend for adopted children. They instantly struck up a friendship. “I saw her nose, her eyes: Everything looked like me,” Ms. Geltink said. Growing up in a small Dutch town, where almost everyone was white, Ms. Geltink said she had been “searching for my identity.” Ms. Tijssen was raised less than 100 miles away. Both said they were close to their adopted families and had grown up with a brother.
image_caption: Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen were born in India and grew up with different adoptive families in the Netherlands. Decades after becoming friends, a DNA test has revealed that the two are also biological sisters.

headline: Iran Is Bracing for Conflict Abroad and at Home
article_summary: Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei’s appointment of hard-line loyalists to top jobs suggests he is prepared to keep the country on a war footing and to quash domestic dissent.
article_body: After almost six months in hiding , Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, has offered the clearest window yet into his vision for ruling the country, appointing a string of hard-line, veteran military commanders to top security roles. The overhaul, which took place this month, signals that he plans to keep the nation on a war footing, analysts say — ready for open-ended confrontation with the United States and for keeping a lid on dissent at home among Iranians suffering the economic brunt of the conflict . The appointments also reflect a leadership that is still struggling to devise a sustainable strategy for deterring Washington, analysts noted, as Tehran seeks a way to end the war without giving up the strategic leverage it has gained, most notably through control over the Strait of Hormuz. The new security leaders will first have to navigate a period of limbo in the conflict. While the large-scale skirmishes have ebbed, neither Washington nor Tehran appears ready to make concessions to reach an agreement over the Strait of Hormuz and a 60-day deadline to agree a deal over Iran’s nuclear program expired on Monday. The standoff has left the region in a state of uncertainty that could erupt into full-scale war again at any moment. Among the appointments made by Ayatollah Khamenei, Mohsen Rezaei , who led the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps during the Iran-Iraq war, was named head of the Supreme National Security Council. And Hossein Taeb, a cleric and former intelligence chief, was tapped to run the Basij, a powerful network of paramilitary forces often used to crush protests. The overhaul also included a new general staff of the armed forces, a new head of the Revolutionary Guards and a commander of the Revolutionary Guards’ naval forces — a critical role as the Strait of Hormuz has become so important. Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, a Washington-based think tank, said, “I would characterize this first and foremost as Mojtaba Khamenei putting his stamp on the national security structure of Iran.” To many Iranians, that stamp looks familiar. Most of Ayatollah Khamenei’s appointees are from an older generation of Iranian leaders who were part of the revolution that established the Islamic Republic in 1979 and were commanders in the Iran-Iraq war in the 1980s. In the course of fighting that war, Ayatollah Khamenei fostered close relationships with some of them , including Mr. Rezaei, who was his commander, and Mr. Taeb, who was in his battalion. “The appointments suggest that, after the enormous vulnerabilities exposed by the war, Mojtaba still trusts the old guard most,” said Omid Memarian, an Iran analyst at DAWN, a Washington-based think tank focused on the Middle East. Some of the appointees, especially Mr. Rezaei, have historically pushed maximalist military aims. He tried and failed to convince Iranian leadership to extend the war with Iraq rather than agreeing to a cease-fire, believing that Iran could have gained more leverage and a better settlement. A similar debate is raging in Iran now about how to end the war with the United States. Moderates in the government, like President Masoud Pezeshkian, say Iran should take advantage of its effective control over the Strait of Hormuz and reach a deal. Hard-liners, however, want to hold out for more concessions and prefer maintaining an aggressive stance that would discourage the United States from launching new military interventions. They note that the last two wars launched by the United States and Israel, in June 2025 and in February this year, began while they were in negotiations with the Trump administration. They also point to the 2015 nuclear deal that Iran agreed with Washington, which President Trump withdrew from in 2018 . Hadi Borhani, a political commentator and professor of Israeli studies at the University of Tehran, said, “The hard-liners gained immense traction, arguing — and history seems to have backed them — that the West is fundamentally untrustworthy.” The hard-liners would also argue, Mr. Borhani added, that the only language the West understands is “resistance, military deterrence, and making any Western intervention in our region prohibitively costly.” Beyond aggressive posturing, Abdolrasool Divsallar, an Iran expert at the Catholic University of Milan, said the appointments reflected Tehran’s struggle to come up with a new approach to deterrence against Washington. Most of the appointees, including Mr. Rezaei, have backed the idea of returning to the short-lived Memorandum of Understanding that was signed with the Trump administration in June. That document was meant to pave the way to an agreement on Iran’s nuclear program. They have also insisted that they will only return to the vaguely worded deal if implemented under Iran’s reading of the terms — in particular, that Tehran should retain control of the Strait of Hormuz until a final deal is agreed rather than giving up that leverage first. “At the bottom of this is a sort of pragmatism, a desire to search for a solution,” Mr. Divsallar said. “It is a desire to guarantee their security.” Ayatollah Khamenei, observers say, has surrounded himself with figures who seem as ready to negotiate, if they deem conditions right, as they are willing to prolong the war when they do not. That is a break with the approach of his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The elder Ayatollah Khamenei, who was killed in the first wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, was wary about negotiating with the United States but restrained in confronting Washington militarily. Under the previous ayatollah, Iran telegraphed missile strikes in response to the Trump administration’s killing of the powerful Quds Force leader, Qassem Soleimani , in 2020. Tehran also gave warning before retaliating after U.S. warplanes joined Israeli strikes on Iran last year. Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has shown a greater willingness to initiate conflict with Washington, some analysts say, pointing to Iran’s decision to start the last round of military skirmishes. He also used belligerent language when announcing his new appointments, including urging Mr. Rezaei to be ready for “powerful offensive operations against the enemy.” Mr. Toossi, the Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, said that “doesn’t mean Iran is turning away from diplomacy with the United States. It suggests a harder approach to diplomacy.” “Iran is willing to engage in negotiations to end the war,” he added, “but is also prepared for a long conflict rather than accept an incomplete or temporary settlement that leaves it vulnerable to renewed U.S. pressure or attack.” The Iranian leadership is apparently gambling that it can do that because Tehran can withstand the economic pain longer than President Trump can endure the fallout of the war in the United States . This strategy has serious implications for Iran’s roughly 90 million people, who are struggling with an economy in free-fall and trapped by the constant risk of a return to all-out war. Dismal conditions fueled a nationwide protests before the war that Iranian security forces crushed with deadly force . The risk of future protests as the economy continues to struggle looms large. “Iranian society increasingly resembles a boiling pot that could erupt with little warning,” said Mr. Memarian, the Iran analyst at DAWN. “A confrontational strategy abroad becomes much easier to sustain if the leadership believes it has the capacity to suppress its political consequences at home.” That is one reason the appointment of Mr. Taeb to head the Basij is notable. He has long been one of Ayatollah Khamenei’s closest allies and had amassed significant power as the head of intelligence for the Revolutionary Guards. The supreme leader’s father dismissed Mr. Taeb as intelligence chief in 2022. Mr. Taeb had become a contentious figure even within the Iranian political system, with Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, a former president, accusing him of fabricating accusations against political opponents. Ayatollah Khamenei called on Mr. Taeb to strengthen the Basij’s “public intelligence network” when he announced his appointment last week, a move that experts say indicates that the group will have an expanded role in domestic surveillance and repression. “Mojtaba may be willing to take risks in confronting the United States that even his father avoided in his final years,” Mr. Memarian said. “The question is whether Iran’s political system — and, more important, Iranian society — can absorb the consequences of that gamble.”

headline: Canadá vuelve a enfrentarse a los aranceles de EE. UU.
article_summary: A menos que los negociadores canadienses logren un acuerdo de última hora, hoy a la medianoche entrarán en vigor una serie de nuevos gravámenes del gobierno Trump.
article_body: Canadá se prepara para el plazo de los aranceles estadounidenses que vence la medianoche del martes, momento en el que entrarán en vigor una serie de nuevos gravámenes del gobierno de Donald Trump, a menos que los negociadores logren un acuerdo de última hora. El representante comercial de Estados Unidos, Jamieson Greer, quien encabeza las conversaciones por la parte estadounidense, dijo la semana pasada que los negociadores estaban evaluando opciones y que esperaba que Canadá retirara ciertas medidas que ya había tomado en respuesta a los aranceles estadounidenses. “Si un país toma represalias contra nosotros, obviamente no vamos a tolerarlo”, dijo Greer a los periodistas en Iowa el viernes. “Vamos a tomar medidas. Mi impresión es que los canadienses quieren tener un enfoque más conciliador, pero ya veremos”. El primer ministro Mark Carney ha instruido a los funcionarios canadienses, que se quedaron en Washington el fin de semana para continuar las conversaciones con sus homólogos estadounidenses, a ofrecer concesiones específicas con el fin tanto de evitar que los nuevos aranceles entren en vigor como de aliviar los gravámenes existentes sobre bienes canadienses clave. Es una tarea difícil. El presidente Trump se ha centrado marcadamente en presionar a Canadá mediante aranceles, y este mes intensificó su retórica beligerante hacia el país, el aliado más cercano y el segundo socio comercial más grande de Estados Unidos, al calificar a su liderazgo de “desagradable” . En comentarios a los medios de comunicación el lunes, Carney dijo que esperaba hablar por teléfono con Trump antes del plazo límite de la medianoche del martes.
image_caption: El Puente Internacional Gordie Howe, que conecta Windsor, Ontario, y Detroit, el día después de su inauguración el mes pasado. El presidente Trump había amenazado con bloquear la apertura del puente.

headline: Trump se acerca a Kim Jong-un y tensa la alianza con Corea del Sur
article_summary: El presidente Trump quiere reducir los ejercicios militares con Corea del Sur, diciendo que eran hostiles hacia Corea del Norte. Pero bajo el mandato de Kim, el Norte se ha vuelto cada vez más beligerante.
article_body: Las fuerzas armadas de Corea del Sur y Estados Unidos consideran que sus ejercicios anuales en Corea del Sur son más cruciales que nunca. Los riesgos han aumentado drásticamente a medida que Corea del Norte ha adquirido experiencia en el campo de batalla con drones y guerra moderna al desplegar tropas para apoyar la guerra de Rusia en Ucrania. El ejercicio de verano apenas había comenzado el lunes cuando el presidente Donald Trump lo condenó públicamente, con lo que asestó otro golpe a la alianza de siete décadas entre Washington y Seúl. Bajo el gobierno de Trump, las relaciones bilaterales ya se han visto sometidas a una inmensa tensión debido a sus aranceles punitivos a las exportaciones surcoreanas. Y su diplomacia transaccional ha frustrado a Corea del Sur, más recientemente cuando pareció poner a Arabia Saudita en camino de enriquecer combustible nuclear en su propio territorio, una exigencia que Seúl ha hecho durante años. En los últimos años, Corea del Norte no solo ha expandido su arsenal nuclear, sino que también ha amenazado repetidamente con usarlo contra Corea del Sur, y ha tachado a su vecino de “enemigo más hostil”. Su líder, Kim Jong-un, también ha forjado un tratado de defensa mutua con Moscú, y ha enviado tropas y armas para apoyar la guerra de Rusia contra Ucrania. A pesar de estas escaladas, Trump, en una publicación en redes sociales , describió a Corea del Norte como “no amenazante y respetuosa” mientras alardeaba de su “muy buena relación” con Kim. En la misma publicación, también criticó las maniobras militares conjuntas de hace décadas con Corea del Sur por ser “no solo costosas” sino “totalmente inapropiadas y hostiles” hacia Corea del Norte.
image_caption: Tropas estadounidenses en Camp Humphreys en Pyeongtaek, Corea del Sur, el lunes. La presencia militar de Estados Unidos en el país ha actuado durante mucho tiempo como un elemento disuasivo para Corea del Norte. Soldados norcoreanos marchando durante un desfile en Moscú en mayo. El líder del Norte, Kim Jong-un, ha forjado un tratado de defensa mutua con Rusia.

headline: Venezuela y Japón después de los terremotos
article_summary: ¿Por qué a algunos países les va mucho mejor que a otros cuando se trata de desastres naturales?
article_body: En junio y julio, megaterremotos azotaron Venezuela y Japón; en las últimas dos semanas, grandes sismos sacudieron Colombia e Indonesia. Es muy pronto para conocer el recuento de los daños de los sismos en Colombia e Indonesia; ambos países siguen escarbando entre los escombros y las cifras de muertos aún no son definitivas. Pero cuando comparas a Venezuela y Japón, hay una diferencia muy sorprendente. En Venezuela, la cifra oficial de muertos supera los 6000; en Japón, es menor a 40. En esta edición escribo sobre por qué a algunos países les va mucho mejor que a otros cuando se trata de desastres naturales. En parte es por el dinero, pero no se trata solo de eso. El 24 de junio, dos terremotos masivos sacudieron Venezuela, y entre ellos pasó aproximadamente medio minuto. Ambos registraron una magnitud superior a siete. Ocurrieron cerca de los principales centros urbanos. Y comenzaron cerca de la superficie de la tierra, lo que significó que el movimiento fue particularmente poderoso . Japón fue azotado por un solo terremoto, cuya magnitud fue de 6,8. Pero el sismo compartió varias similitudes con los de Venezuela. Su poca profundidad también produjo un movimiento intenso; su epicentro también estuvo cerca de zonas densamente pobladas.

headline: U.S. and Iran Blow Through Deadline to Agree to a Broad Deal to End War
article_summary: President Trump said a cease-fire agreed in June would lead to limits on Iran’s nuclear program and finish the conflict, but the countries appear far apart.
article_body: The United States and Iran on Monday missed their 60-day deadline to reach a deal to curtail Iran’s nuclear program under the terms of the cease-fire they agreed to in June, underlining the breakdown of a truce that President Trump promised would end the war. Mr. Trump had announced the so-called memorandum of understanding between the two countries with great fanfare two months ago. But the short-lived agreement failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran effectively blockaded after Israel and the United States attacked in late February, or end a conflict that has entered its sixth month. The expiration of the deadline is largely symbolic, as both Mr. Trump and Iran’s leaders have said in recent weeks that the deal is basically dead. The original deal also provided for the 60-day period to be extended if necessary, which would have been likely given the sensitive and complex nature of the negotiations. But the milestone nonetheless shows how Mr. Trump has struggled to achieve his war aims — like forcing Iran to curtail its nuclear ambitions — and how emboldened the Iranian government feels, with the two countries at risk of further military conflict. The president said on Monday that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon was still his main objective. “The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon,” he said on social media. Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, had told reporters earlier that the negotiations on the nuclear deal “never began,” adding that the 60-day period was “fundamentally no longer relevant.” There have been no publicly reported U.S. strikes on Iranian targets since late July. But the United States and Iran appear to be gearing up for a protracted campaign of economic attrition that could easily tip over into renewed warfare, analysts said. Iran is wielding its control of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for oil and gas shipping, to choke global energy markets, raising pressure on Mr. Trump to reach a deal. The Trump administration has rescinded the sanctions waivers on Iranian oil, which it issued during the brief truce. U.S. forces have also reimposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports, hoping that squeezing Iran economically will force it to make concessions. But Iran’s leaders are betting that the country can endure more economic pain than the United States, especially as Mr. Trump faces midterm elections in November. “The Islamic republic is trying to put the economic crunch on America, and America is trying to put the economic crunch on the Islamic republic,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, an Iran expert at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington-based research institute. Mr. Taleblu said that the U.S. economic campaign could be punishingly effective against the Iranian economy. But Iran’s clerical leadership was likely to respond by escalating further, he warned, setting the stage for another round of armed conflict. Like Mr. Trump’s other recent Middle East deals, the June agreement aimed at a quick truce while pushing off thornier dilemmas for future rounds of negotiations. Analysts argued that the vaguely worded agreement was tilted in Iran’s favor and suggested that the president was trying to wind down an increasingly unpopular war that threatened to bog him down in the Middle East. Talks over Iran’s nuclear program were delayed for what were supposed to be two months of further talks, even though Mr. Trump had said concern that Iran might obtain a nuclear weapon was a major element of his case for war. U.S. officials hoped the deal would at least reopen the Strait of Hormuz, to ease the pressure on the global economy. But the cease-fire faltered almost immediately, and Iran quickly moved to assert its control over the waterway. Iranian officials cited ambiguous language in the cease-fire deal to declare that some ships were wrongly passing through the waterway without their permission and fired on some. U.S. forces retaliated by bombarding southern Iran , prompting a cycle of attacks and counterattacks. The escalation prompted Mr. Trump to consider launching a major military offensive against Iran on at least two occasions. He pulled back both times after pleas from regional allies like Saudi Arabia, which have borne the brunt of Iranian military reprisals, as well as warnings from White House advisers over dwindling stockpiles of critical munitions .
image_caption: People in Tehran, Iran, last month. Iranians are coping with severe economic strain from six months of war.

headline: Mushroom Murder Case Returns to Court as Convicted Killer Appeals
article_summary: An Australian woman, Erin Patterson, was found guilty of murdering three of her husband’s relatives and trying to kill a fourth by serving them deadly mushrooms.
article_body: An Australian woman who was found guilty of murdering three of her husband’s relatives and attempting to murder a fourth, by serving them a beef Wellington laced with poisonous mushrooms, is expected to appeal her conviction on Wednesday. Erin Patterson, 51, was convicted of the crimes last year after a two-month trial that captivated the nation. The case, which became known as the “mushroom murders,” featured in daily podcasts, television series and books. The case centered on a lunch in 2023 that took place in the rural town of Leongatha, in the state of Victoria. Ms. Patterson had invited her estranged husband, Simon Patterson, who declined to attend. But his parents, Gail and Don Patterson, went, along with Gail’s sister, Heather Wilkinson, and her husband, Ian Wilkinson. Within a week of the lunch, three of the group were dead. They had symptoms indicative of poisoning by death cap mushrooms. Mr. Wilkinson fell critically ill but survived, and later testified at Ms. Patterson’s trial.
image_caption: Erin Patterson leaving court in Melbourne, Australia, last year. Ian Wilkinson, the only one of four guests to have survived the lunch hosted by Ms. Patterson, outside a court in Melbourne last year.

headline: Young Women Joined Protests in India. The Hate Followed.
article_summary: Widespread online abuse and visits from the police show the added risks women take standing up for their beliefs in a patriarchal society.
article_body: Rhiya Ahir went viral after an image circulated of her blocking a police van that was carrying detained protesters last month during India’s ongoing youth agitation. A vast army of online trolls has stalked her since. They called it a play for attention by Ms. Ahir, 27, a Mumbai-based model and actor. They insinuated that she sold sexually explicit content behind a paywall on Instagram. They circulated a video of her diving into the sea in a bikini. They flooded her social media accounts with slurs and rape threats. Ms. Ahir has chosen to rise above it. “You’re not scared of someone who is telling you online that ‘I’m going to rip you apart the day I see you,’” she said. “I’m trying not to reply to any of them, just letting them do their thing and show their face to the world.” Thousands of young women have participated in nationwide protests demanding accountability from the government for a flawed education system. But in the two months since the demonstrations started, they have been doxxed and bombarded online by people who have called them immoral, threatened sexual abuse and acid attacks, and used artificial intelligence to create demeaning images. A majority of the attacks have come from accounts, many anonymous, that push Hindu right-wing ideology and pitch themselves as custodians of religious morality. But high-profile politicians, commentators and outraged individuals have chimed in. In a series of Instagram messages, Kangana Ranaut, a well-known Bollywood actress and member of Parliament from the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Hindu nationalist political party of Prime Minister Narendra Modi , called out a “new generation of so-called westernized Indian women.” She labeled them “Generation Gutter,” saying they had “nothing to offer the system” but were too “corrupt and ugly” to be “home makers.”
image_caption: Rhiya Ahir has suffered constant online abuse from trolls after an image of her at a protest in Mumbai last month went viral. Ms. Ahir blocking a police van carrying detained protesters in Mumbai, India, last month.

headline: As Economic Pessimism Spreads, China’s Worker-Writers Strike a Chord
article_summary: Poems, essays and books written by working-class writers have garnered recognition in recent years — as well as increasing government attention.
article_body: A Chinese food delivery driver rushes from gig to gig, measuring time by the number of jobs he completes instead of by the passing of the seasons. He toils in cities across China to send money back to his family, but has been away for so long that his son calls him “that man” instead of “Dad.” These are scenes from the poems of Wang Jibing, a food delivery driver, one of several Chinese poets and authors who have turned their experiences of repetitive factory labor and insecure gig work into art. This literary genre has ballooned in popularity in recent years, as many Chinese have grown pessimistic about the economy. For a wide swath of society, wages have stagnated, youth unemployment is high and the promise of a better life in return for hard work has faded. Some authors use their writing to call attention to the harsh realities of life for migrant and gig workers, while others celebrate the humanity that flourishes in spite of those conditions. Their styles are often raw and straightforward. Writers like Hu Anyan, a courier who wrote a best-selling memoir about the jobs he has worked across the gig economy, and Fan Yusu, who left her children behind to work as a live-in nanny in Beijing, have tapped into these themes. They have published essays online that have been shared widely and led to book deals. Some best-sellers have been translated and published overseas. Last month, Mr. Wang’s new poetry collection, “Low Flight,” won the Lu Xun Literary Prize, in the highest institutional recognition for the genre yet. For the Chinese public, curiosity about these workers is intertwined with anxiety about their own prospects. The concern may be particularly pronounced for members of China’s middle class. They “pay more attention to these kinds of narratives because they may represent their future lives,” said Zhu Ping, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of California San Diego’s literature department.
image_caption: Hu Anyan’s memoir, “I Deliver Parcels in Beijing,” became a best seller in China and was later translated into English. It is a diaristic account of the 19 jobs he held over two decades across China.

headline: Bou Meng, Rare Survivor of Khmer Rouge Torture House, Dies at 85
article_summary: Saved by his ability to paint, he was one of only a handful of prisoners to make it out of the brutal prison Tuol Sleng.
article_body: Bou Meng, a Cambodian painter who was one of only a handful of prisoners to survive the Khmer Rouge interrogation and torture house Tuol Sleng, and who later became a fixture at the genocide museum on the site, died on Friday at his home in the village of Thommeak Trai in Kandal Province, Cambodia, about 30 miles from the capital, Phnom Penh. He was 85. The death was announced by the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum. The cause was complications of a stroke he suffered earlier this year. Late in his life, Mr. Bou Meng was one of four living symbols of the Khmer Rouge atrocities that left 1.7 million people dead between 1975 and 1979. Together with another Tuol Sleng survivor who returned to the prison, a mechanic named Chum Mey, he personified the victims. A few miles down the road, the last two surviving leaders of the Khmer Rouge regime were tried. They were convicted of crimes against humanity in 2014 and of genocide in 2018; Nuon Chea died in 2019 , and Khieu Samphan remains in prison. Some 14,000 people were arrested and interrogated at Tuol Sleng, also known as S-21, and almost all were sent to a killing field. As Huy Vannak describes in his 2010 biography, “Bou Meng: A Survivor From Khmer Rouge Prison S-21,” Mr. Bou Meng was spared, after two months of imprisonment and seven days of torture, when a guard called out to a group of shackled prisoners, “Can anyone paint pictures?” Mr. Bou Meng was assigned to paint portraits of the Khmer Rouge leader Pol Pot, as well as of Marx and Lenin, fearing for his life if he made a mistake. Another painter who survived Tuol Sleng, Vann Nath, died in 2011 .
image_caption: Bou Meng, who was imprisoned at the notorious Khmer Rouge interrogation and torture facility Tuol Sleng, in 2009 at the prison, which became a genocide museum.

headline: An Isolated Corner of Colombia Faces Deeper Hardship After a Quake An Isolated Corner of Colombia Faces Deeper Hardship After a Quake
article_body: In Colombia’s remote Pacific region of Chocó, isolation has long been a fact of life. Roads are few, electricity and health care are limited, and much of the population lives in poverty while armed groups control parts of the territory. Then came the earthquake. Already one of the country’s most vulnerable areas, Chocó was also the epicenter of a 7.4-magnitude quake that struck last week, killing at least 298 people across the country. In Chocó, the full extent of the devastation is unknown, as the authorities struggle to reach communities scattered across the region. Now, Chocó faces a reconstruction effort that will have to overcome the same geographic, economic and political barriers that have shaped the region for generations. “We were left in ruins,” said Juan Fernando Taborda, 35, who does odd jobs in La Ye, a town of about 600 people two hours from Quibdó, the capital of Chocó, where most buildings were destroyed or damaged. “We have nothing.” For much of Colombia’s history, Chocó was a remote mining frontier where enslaved Africans were brought by the Spanish to work in the mines. Some escaped and formed communities beyond colonial control.
image_caption: Soldiers and volunteers offloading aid supplies from a helicopter in San José del Palmar, Colombia, a remote town close to the earthquake’s epicenter. People grabbing items from damaged buildings in La Ye, Colombia.

headline: Israeli Strikes in Lebanon Kill 11, Health Officials Say
article_summary: The Lebanese health ministry said children were among those killed. The Israeli prime minister’s office said Hezbollah had struck first, injuring three Israeli soldiers.
article_body: A pair of Israeli strikes killed at least 11 people in southern Lebanon early Saturday, the Lebanese health ministry said, one of the deadliest attacks in the country since a fragile truce took effect nearly two months ago. A strike overnight in Ansar, near the city of Nabatieh, killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two others, health ministry officials said. Hours later, Israeli warplanes carried out an airstrike on Deir al-Zahrani, killing at least four and wounding 17 others, according to the ministry. The Israeli military said in a statement that its attacks in the Ansar area had targeted infrastructure belonging to Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group. It did not respond to a request for comment on the reports of civilian deaths or on the attack later on Saturday morning. Nawaf Salam, Lebanon’s prime minister, called the escalation on Saturday “extremely dangerous” and said it undermined efforts to establish stability in the country’s south. “The seven martyrs in the Israeli strike on Ansar town were not ‘military infrastructure,’ and the children and women killed were not military targets,” Mr. Nawaf said on social media . The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said later on Saturday that Hezbollah had attacked Israeli soldiers inside Lebanon, seriously injuring three of them. The military, it said in a statement, then struck the group’s “headquarters which ordered the attack” and only later learned “that Hezbollah deliberately put civilians in that military compound.”
image_caption: The aftermath of an Israeli strike in Deir al-Zahrani, a town in southern Lebanon, on Saturday.

headline: Trump’s Other Hold on the Americas: The Visa
article_summary: As part of its expansionist approach to the Western Hemisphere, the Trump administration is trying to reassert its dominance, one U.S. visa at a time.
article_body: When Chilean officials signed an authorization for a 12,000-mile undersea cable connecting the country to Hong Kong, they were thrilled. They said the Chinese project would boost national connectivity and even reach Chile’s remote Easter Island. But the mood shifted abruptly later that day in January after a senior official from the U.S. Embassy in Santiago met with Guillermo Petersen, the chief of cabinet at Chile’s telecommunications ministry. According to Mr. Petersen, the American official warned that the project could increase the risk of Chinese cyberattacks and that, if Chile forged ahead, the United States would issue a travel ban not only for the officials involved, but for their spouses and children as well. Across Latin America, the Trump administration has deployed aggressive tactics to tighten its grip on the region. They include crippling tariffs and economic sanctions , strikes on dozens of boats in the Caribbean and Pacific, wading into foreign elections and the capture of the president of a nation in his own capital. But one of its most agile and surgical tools is also deeply personal: the U.S. visa. The meeting in Chile lasted just six minutes, Mr. Petersen said. But that was enough to persuade his government to put the project on hold. “It was basically a threat,” Claudio Araya, then Chile’s telecommunications under secretary, said this month.
image_caption: The State Department overseen by Marco Rubio has restored the visas of political figures in Central America once penalized by the U.S. government and has revoked visas for others. Claudio Araya was Chile’s telecommunications under secretary when U.S. officials threatened to revoke visas because of a Chinese undersea-cable project.
